no line of STACK_SITEMAP.md, STACK_PLANNING.md or CLOUD_V1.md (grepped 2026-08-23). §38 calls itself a "Final architecture ruling", but in this tree a ruling is an R-number. E needs one, particularly because of (2).

2. Findings

Severity: BLOCKER = the system cannot run as specified · HIGH = silent incorrectness · MED = a gap that will cost a round · LOW = worth knowing.

A — internal contradictions

A1 · BLOCKER · event_id is a ULID in §8 and a UUID in §12 — FIXED

§8's envelope shows "event_id": "01J..." (a ULID: Crockford base32, 26 chars). §12 declares event_id UUID. toUUID('01JABC…') throws — the first insert fails, and nothing before that point reveals it. batch_id has the same conflict between §13 and §12.

Resolved as UUIDv7, which keeps every property the ULID was chosen for (client-generated, time-sortable, no coordination) while fitting the UUID column at 16 bytes instead of 26. The alternative — keep ULIDs, declare FixedString(26) — is equally coherent and costs 10 bytes/row. This is a decision to confirm, not one I should settle. See packages/e-schema/ids.mjs.

A2 · BLOCKER · The idempotency the brief requires is not achievable with the schema it specifies — FIXED

This is the largest defect, and it is structural rather than a typo.

§14 mandates pull → insert → confirmed → ack, which is correct — the alternative loses data. That ordering deliberately creates a window in which a worker inserts, dies, and its message is redelivered. §28 test 16 then requires: "Worker crash after DB insert but before ACK is safe/idempotent."

Nothing in the brief deduplicates anything. §12 specifies ENGINE = MergeTree, which has no deduplication. insert_deduplication_token appears nowhere in the document.

Two further facts, neither of which the brief states:

  • On ClickHouse Cloud, ENGINE = MergeTree is silently substituted with SharedMergeTree,

which is replicated and therefore can deduplicate. That substitution is the only reason test 16 could ever pass — and it still requires the token to be set, which nothing does.

  • The same DDL anywhere else — a local container, CI, self-hosted — gets a plain unreplicated

MergeTree with no deduplication at all. So the test would pass in production and fail locally, for a reason invisible in the schema.

Resolved in packages/e-clickhouse/insert.mjs, and it takes three parts, all required:

  1. a deterministic dedup token derived from batch_id (which §13 already guarantees is stable);

  2. deterministic row order before blocking — ClickHouse dedups per block, and Cloudflare

Queues does not guarantee order, so a redelivery that reorders rows would split them into different blocks and dedup would silently miss. (The Cloud lane already paid for assuming queue order once — R41.)

  1. a bounded block count, because the dedup window is finite and overrunning it makes dedup

stop working with no error anywhere. (Round 1 wrote "default 1000 blocks" here as if it were a fact. It was an assumption, and round 2's N4 replaced it with declare-then-verify — see §5.2.)

Falsifiers in test/flush.test.mjs, including §28.16-DEFECT, which runs the crash scenario against the brief's design as written and asserts that it does double-count — six rows for three events, invisible to a DISTINCT count.

A3 · BLOCKER · PARTITION BY on a client-controlled timestamp is a queue-poisoning DoS — FIXED

§8 makes occurred_at a browser field. §12 partitions the table by it. A client sending events spread across 230 years produces ~2,800 partitions from one batch, which exceeds ClickHouse's max_partitions_per_insert_block (default 100) and fails the whole insert — including every valid event in it. Under §14's ack-last rule the poison batch is then never acked, and it redelivers on every flush forever, blocking the pipeline behind it.

Unauthenticated browser input, one request, permanent stall.

Resolved three ways: partition by received_at (our clock), clamp occurred_at at ingest to [received − 7d, received + 1h], and store occurred_at_clamped so a clamp is itself data — a rise in it is either a broken client or an attempt.

A4 · MED · §15 proposes D1; R7 removed D1 from the architecture

CLAUDE.md's standing direction: "R7 has since removed D1 from the architecture: Pigsty owns application state, and D1 holds none." §15 lists D1 among the snapshot-store candidates. Resolved: the prototype uses KV, which is the right shape regardless — one key, written once per flush, read on every page load.

A5 · LOW · The /live route contradicts the brief's own honesty rule

§21 creates /live and, four paragraphs later, says "Do not market V1 features as live"; §28 test 39 is the falsifier for a problem introduced on the same page. Suggest /pipeline or /architecture until the Durable Object plane in §23 actually exists.

A6 · HIGH · The vendor fanout point makes PostHog useless for what PostHog is for

§17 puts PostHog/Amplitude fanout after the ClickHouse insert — i.e. inside the 2-hour flush. Every vendor event therefore arrives ≥2h late, which breaks PostHog session stitching. Meanwhile §9 says PostHog also receives its own direct high-resolution browser path. So PostHog sees the same user action twice, by two paths, ~2 hours apart. §17's dedup instruction ("use stable E event_id downstream") only works if the direct browser path also carries E's event_id — which the brief never requires and the SDK has no reason to do.

Not resolved in the prototype — this is an architecture decision. The options are: fan out from the ingest worker instead (immediate, but couples acceptance to vendor availability); fan out from a separate queue consumer (a second push consumer that doesn't touch ClickHouse); or accept the delay and drop PostHog's direct path. Recommend the middle one.

A7 · HIGH · Storing a consent object does not say what consent.analytics: false means — FIXED

§8 puts consent in the envelope and §12 stores it in ClickHouse. The brief never states what happens when it is false. Both readings are bad: reject at ingest (then why is the field stored?), or store it — which persists analytics data for a user who declined analytics, i.e. the precise thing consent exists to prevent.

Resolved: consent gates. analytics !== true is refused at ingest with consent_withheld, nothing is stored, and the SDK defaults consent to denied so an integration that forgets to set it collects nothing rather than everything.

A8 · MED · A GDPR erasure path over a plain MergeTree is a table rewrite — FIXED

§25 requires "a deletion path by opaque identity" and "retention policy configuration". §12's DDL has neither lightweight deletes nor a TTL, so erasure is an ALTER TABLE … DELETE mutation that rewrites parts. Resolved: allow_experimental_lightweight_delete = 1 and a 25-month TTL on received_at in ddl.sql.

A9 · HIGH · The cron cliff, made lethal — FOUND BY THE BATTERY, FIXED

Not in the brief; found while building the prototype, in the prototype's own flush worker. Kept because it is the most dangerous shape in the design.

A Cron Trigger gets 15 min CPU at an interval ≥ 1 hour and 30 seconds below it. The flush worker reserves time before its deadline so an in-flight insert can finish. With a fixed 60 s reserve against a 30 s budget, the deadline lands in the past: the pull loop exits on its first check, reports success, and flushes nothing — on every run, forever. The queue then grows until retention expires and the platform silently discards everything.

The failure is reachable by editing one cron expression for fresher data, which §6 actively invites. And it hides inside its own normal case: ok: true, queue_drained, 0 events is exactly what a healthy idle pipeline looks like.

Resolved: the reserve scales with the budget, and a budget below a floor refuses loudly with budget_too_small rather than doing nothing quietly.

B — external facts, checked 2026-08-23

#Brief's claimVerdict
B1§7 · "Queue operations are metered in 64 KB chunks"Correct. "Each 64 KB of data written, read, or deleted" = one billable operation. The <64 KB target is well-founded.
B2§5 · "Pull batch size supports up to 100 messages"Correct — matches the documented max consumer batch size.
B3§5 · "Paid retention configurable up to 14 days"**Correct, but it is configured, not default.** A queue left at its default sits inside §6's CRITICAL band (8h) rather than far outside it. Phase 3's "paid retention configured" is load-bearing; keep it.
B4§13 · "hard max bytes"Never given a number. The wall is 128 KB per message. The prototype rejects at 96 KB at ingest, leaving room for the fields the worker adds, so our own additions can never be what breaches the platform limit.
B5§5 · why a push consumer can't buffer 2hThe argument is right but not the strongest one. §5 reasons from delivery delay. The decisive fact is that max_batch_timeout caps at 60 seconds — a push consumer cannot be configured to buffer for two hours at all. Worth stating, because it turns a judgement call into a constraint.
B6Cron CPU budgetNot mentioned anywhere. 15 min at ≥1h interval, 30 s below. See A9.
B7§14 · "until time budget reached"Budget never named. 15 min wall clock; visibility timeout max 12h; consumer wall clock 15 min. All compatible with the 2h design — worth writing down since §14 depends on a number it doesn't state.
B8§12 · ENGINE = MergeTreeClickHouse Cloud does substitute SharedMergeTree, and it is replicated. Load-bearing for A2, and unstated.
B9§10/§16 · ClickHouse Cloud Basic pricesCould not verify — clickhouse.com/pricing is client-rendered and returns no figures to a fetch. Not disputed; not confirmed either. §16's own instruction ("Do not promise these numbers. Measure them.") is the right discipline — keep it and re-check first-party before any published claim.

C — gaps

  • C1 · HIGH · R4 conflict. See §0.2 above.

  • C2 · MED · E is in no planning doc. See §0.1 above.

  • C3 · MED · No DNS. e.computedriven.com is NXDOMAIN.

  • C4 · HIGH · No privacy policy exists anywhere in the portfolio, and no consent mechanism.

§25 says "privacy documentation based on implementation" — correct, and it means the first /_e/* route cannot ship until at least one privacy page exists. Because §20's pattern rolls the same endpoint across ~21 sites, this becomes every site's obligation at once. This is the practical gate on Phase 2, and the brief does not identify it as one.

  • C5 · HIGH · §20's anti-spoofing rule sits beside a schema that contradicts it — FIXED.

§20 says derive site_id from the route; §8's envelope still carries it as a client field. A rule in prose next to a schema that disagrees is a rule that gets lost. Resolved structurally: the client's value is not validated, it is overwritten, and the SDK does not send it at all.

  • C6 · MED · No privacy-signal handling.

CORRECTED 2026-08-23 (round 2, N9). This line originally read "No `Sec-GPC` / `doNotTrack` handling — FIXED". Only Sec-GPC was implemented. Claiming two and shipping one is the exact failure this register exists to catch, and it was caught on review rather than here. They are also not interchangeable: GPC is a deliberate, legally meaningful opt-out, while DNT is deprecated and was historically sent on-by-default — which is why the industry stopped honouring it and why GPC exists at all. Now: both are honoured, as a stated policy (HONOUR_SEC_GPC / HONOUR_DNT in limits.mjs), because E's payload is entirely optional analytics and there is no product function lost by over-honouring. The response names which signal opted the request out.

  • C7 · MED · The §19 journey token is replayable. No algorithm named, no key rotation, no

jti. A signed token with only iat/exp can be replayed inside its window to link an unrelated visitor into someone else's journey — which falsifies §28 test 32. Not resolved; needs a single-use marker or a binding to the destination session. Flagged for GPT.

  • C8 · MED · No ingest response contract — FIXED. No status code, CORS policy, or body was

specified. The prototype returns 202 with {accepted, rejected}, a restrictive origin allowlist on the fallback endpoint only, and no-store.

  • C9 · LOW · §30's cost dashboard needs inputs §15 forbids it from fetching. The cost panel's

numbers must be computed at flush time and written into the snapshot; nothing says who does it.

  • C10 · LOW · §3's numbered list is `1. 2. 3. 3. 3. 3. …` — fifteen items, thirteen numbered 3.

Renders fine; the source is wrong, and it makes the questions impossible to cite by number.

3. What the prototype is

prototype/ — zero dependencies, node --test, 55 passing falsifiers.

packages/e-schema/      limits.mjs (every platform number, CITED vs CHOSEN, with dates)
                        ids.mjs · vocabulary.mjs · envelope.mjs (validate/redact/clamp)
packages/e-sdk/         sdk.mjs — microbatcher, consent gating, identity lifecycle
packages/e-clickhouse/  ddl.sql (4 corrections, annotated) · insert.mjs (the A2 closure)
workers/cd-e-ingest/    edge acceptance · site_id derived from route
workers/cd-e-flush/     the 2h drain · insert→confirm→ack · A9 guard
test/                   fakes.mjs + 3 suites, mapped to §28's numbered falsifiers

The design rule throughout: every platform touch point is injected, so the acceptance path and the drain algorithm are testable without a Cloudflare account. test/fakes.mjs models a queue that redelivers, reorders and expires leases, and a ClickHouse that deduplicates and can be constructed not to — which is how A2 is demonstrated rather than asserted.

Run it:

cd e.computedriven.com/prototype && npm test

5. Round 2 — hardening

Travis reviewed the round-1 prototype, independently reran the battery, and ruled: keep Workers + Queues + ClickHouse; one more adversarial round before deploying anything. What follows is that round.

5.1 Decisions ruled

#Decision
1ClickHouse Cloud is a narrow, explicit exception to R4 — not a repeal. E is an isolated analytical data plane with no product or control-plane authority. Needs its own revision-register entry; see §5.5.
2UUIDv7 approved. 16-byte native ClickHouse UUID, client-generatable, time-ordered. A1 is closed.
3Privacy is a deployment gate, rolled out one site at a time. computedriven.com first; observe; then expand. Do not touch ~21 repos at once.
4A2/A3 approved in principle — deterministic dedup token, deterministic row ordering, received_at partitioning, occurred_at clamped and the clamp recorded.
5A6 resolved with a second, immediate vendor queue. See §5.3.
6C7 (cross-domain journey tokens) deferred. When built: single-use jti, bound to destination/session, backed by a Durable Object rather than KV because one-time redemption wants strong consistency.

5.2 Findings sent back, and what was done

#FindingStatus
N1The ingest acknowledgment boundary. ctx.waitUntil(queue.send()) is non-blocking and its send errors are implicitly ignored, so round 1's 202 meant only "we parsed it". The browser then discarded its batch on a promise that was never made.FIXED — await both sends before answering; a failure returns 503 naming the batch_id to retry with.
N2Batch identity was owned by the wrong side. The SDK emptied its buffer before transport succeeded, and the Worker minted a fresh batch_id per HTTP request — while ClickHouse dedup keys on batch_id. A browser retry therefore produced a batch identical in every field except the one dedup depends on, with stable event_ids that nothing was comparing.FIXED — the SDK generates batch_id once, holds the batch until confirmed, and retries the same ids; the Worker validates and preserves, and refuses a malformed one rather than replacing it. Pending buffer is bounded and drops are counted.
N3The browser was authoritative for authenticated identity. Round 1's envelope accepted user_id/account_id straight from an unauthenticated client.FIXED — browser is authoritative for anonymous_id/session_id/journey_id only. user_id/account_id come from a signed identity assertion minted by the auth boundary and verified at ingest. A client that declares them is rejected, not stripped — stripping leaves a misconfigured integration shipping data that looks exactly like a site with no logged-in users. Mirrors R21 exactly.
N4The dedup window was an unverified assumption. Round 1 hard-coded 1000 blocks "the default"; ClickHouse's current guidance says 100. Correctness must not rest on either.FIXED — declare (conservatively, at 100) → read system.merge_tree_settings → guard with min(declared, actual) → publish it in every flush snapshot. An unreadable setting is recorded, not silently assumed.
N5`allow_experimental_lightweight_delete = 1` is stale, and the 25-month TTL was being canonised as a technical constant.FIXED — flag removed. TTL kept but marked UNRULED: it is a privacy/product decision, and it must be the same number the privacy page publishes.
N6Cron edge case. The deadline was checked once per pull, then up to 100 messages ran sequentially — a pull starting just inside the deadline could overrun the invocation window.FIXED — deadline checked per message, with bounded concurrency (default 8).
N7Benchmark the concurrency.DONE — bench/concurrency.mjs sweeps 1/4/8/16/32 and reports active-minutes per million events, the unit the cost goal is in. Refuses to be quoted without --live.
N8Vendor dedup keys.DONE, and PostHog is not what was assumed — see §5.4.
N9Claim discipline: "Sec-GPC / doNotTrack — FIXED" when only GPC shipped.FIXED — C6 corrected in place; both signals now honoured as a declared policy, and the response names which one fired.
N10Attribution values were unbounded. A query-string key allowlist says nothing about values: ?utm_campaign=travis@example.com and a megabyte of garbage both passed round 1 untouched. source_domain is LowCardinality(String) — a type whose whole argument is a small distinct set.FIXED — hostname normalisation, length caps on UTM/referrer/path, and value-level scrubbing of emails, JWTs and key-shaped runs.

5.3 A6 resolved — two queues

                           ┌─► e-events-clickhouse
                           │   PULL consumer · ~2h batches   → ClickHouse sleeps
Browser ─► cd-e-ingest ────┤
                           └─► e-events-vendors
                               PUSH consumer · ~10s          → PostHog · Amplitude

One active consumer per queue, which is also why this cannot be expressed as two consumers on one queue. cd-e-ingest writes to both and awaits both before 202. A partial failure returns 503 and the browser retries — which is only safe because of N2: the same batch_id dedups the ClickHouse leg and the same event_id dedups the vendor leg. Round 1 could not have offered this.

5.4 The PostHog result — verified, and it is not Amplitude's story

Checked against PostHog's own documentation rather than assumed:

  • Dedup is on the four-tuple (uuid, event name, timestamp, distinct_id) — all four must

match. A retry that regenerates the timestamp does not deduplicate, which is why the SDK freezes occurred_at at track() time and nothing downstream rewrites it.

  • It is eventual — it happens during background ClickHouse merges, so duplicates are visible

for a while regardless.

  • PostHog states it is not guaranteed, "due to how merges work in ClickHouse".

Amplitude is the clean case: insert_id is a documented dedup key, and E's immutable event_id maps straight onto it.

So: send all four members stably, and treat PostHog dedup as hygiene, not a guarantee. No E correctness claim rests on it. This is what brief §1's "PostHog and Amplitude are downstream analytical lenses, not sources of truth" costs in practice — and it is worth knowing before someone reconciles two dashboards and concludes the pipeline is broken.

5.5 Revision-register entry — needs a number claimed at paste time

REVISION_REGISTER.md was at R43 when round 1 began and R74 four hours later — two sessions are appending to it live, and my memory records ruling numbers colliding with a parallel session before. So the entry is written here rather than pasted into a table another session is actively extending. Claim the next free number at paste time; do not trust the one below.

| R75 | **E is an isolated analytical data plane, and a narrow exception to R4.** ClickHouse Cloud is admitted as a third provider for E ONLY. E holds no product or control-plane authority: it may not be read by authorization, entitlement, billing or World logic, and the product plane must never require a read from it to function. R4 stands unrepealed everywhere else — "Cloudflare for everything; Fly keeps only Keycloak" — and this entry is the exception that proves it is still being enforced rather than quietly eroded. The reason for the exception is the reason ClickHouse was chosen: an independent scale and failure domain, and learning the analytics stack while mistakes are cheap | 2026-08-23 | Travis |

5.6 Two findings the round-2 battery found in round 2's own work

Both were introduced by the fix for N10 — the change that exists to handle hostile input.

N11 · HIGH · ReDoS in the redactor. The first draft's email pattern used an unbounded local part ([A-Z0-9._%+-]+@). A long run containing no @ makes the engine match the whole run, fail, and backtrack one character at a time — O(n²). One megabyte of A is ~10¹² steps, inside the function whose entire job is processing hostile browser input, on a Worker with a 30-second CPU limit. It hung the test runner, which is how it was found: a test written for something else. Fixed two ways, since either alone is thin — quantifiers are bounded, and redactValue truncates before it scans.

N12 · MED · The redactor ate the data it exists to protect. The first draft redacted any 32+ character run of [A-Za-z0-9_-]. That class includes hyphens, and summer-sale-2026-north-america-launch is 37 characters — so the redactor would have silently destroyed the attribution values E exists to collect, in the field most likely to carry them. Fixed with an explicit entropy test (mixed case and a digit) instead of length alone. The tradeoff is now stated in the code rather than implied: a credential that happens to be all-lowercase with no digits still gets through, and that is the conservative side of a judgement, not an oversight.

Both are the same shape as A9 in round 1 — the defect was in the thing built to prevent the previous defect. That is now three rounds running, and it is worth naming as a pattern rather than noticing it again next time.

5.7 What is still open

  • C7 — cross-domain journey token replay. Deferred by decision; not needed to instrument one site.

  • §10/§16 ClickHouse prices — still unverified; the pricing page is client-rendered and returns

no figures to a fetch. Do not publish a cost claim from them.

  • §36 Q12/Q13 — does Basic actually scale to zero under this workload, and what active-minutes

per day does a 2h cadence produce. Unanswerable without spending money; they are the first things the deployment should measure.

  • The TTL (N5) and the `INSERT_CONCURRENCY` default (N7) are both placeholders awaiting a

real decision and a real measurement respectively.

6. Round 3 — implementation hardening

Travis read the round-2 prototype rather than its findings, reran the battery independently (107/107), and raised eight further findings. The architecture was reaffirmed: keep Workers + Queues + ClickHouse. One of these findings retracts a justification round 2 wrote down as fact.

6.1 The findings

#FindingStatus
N13The insert strategy was fighting ClickHouse, on a premise that was false. Round 2 set async_insert: 0 and justified it: "it would ack to us before the data is durable". Verified false — wait_for_async_insert defaults to 1, and ClickHouse "only acknowledges the insert after the data is successfully flushed to disk". Round 2 disabled a correct mechanism on a misunderstanding and then recorded the misunderstanding as a reason, which is worse than the setting. The shape mattered too: browser batches cap at ~25 events and the flush inserts one message at a time, so ROWS_PER_BLOCK = 10_000 never split a single block — every insert was ≤25 rows, and thousands of tiny parts per flush create merge pressure that keeps a supposedly sleeping service awake.FIXED — async_insert: 1, wait_for_async_insert: 1, set explicitly. Plus a version floor: dedup applies to async inserts only from a recent enough server, so supportsAsyncInsertDedup() is checked each flush and published. Without it, the fix for N13 would have silently reintroduced A2.
N14**There was no session model, only a session id.** The SDK minted anonymous_id and session_id in its constructor with no persistence, so every document was a new visitor and a new session — on a portfolio of static multi-page sites, where every funnel spans documents.FIXED — first-party persistence (after consent), session_id is a UUIDv7 minted at session start, 30-minute inactivity gap, 24-hour ceiling, throttled heartbeat so a synchronous localStorage write does not land on every click.
N15Identity was read at SEND time, not frozen at SEAL time — with a reproduced witness. User A's batch fails and stays pending; A logs out, B logs in; the retry goes up under B's assertion. A subtler variant: identify() created no batch boundary, so pre-login and post-login events shared one batch and ingest stamped authenticated identity onto events that were anonymous when they happened.FIXED — the assertion is captured into the immutable sealed batch and never re-read; identify() seals first. And the deeper repair: E no longer rewrites history at all — see §6.2.
N16`sendBeacon` quietly reopened N1's hole. Round 2 established that 202 means both queue writes succeeded, then used sendBeacon on pagehide and treated its true as confirmation, deleting the batch. sendBeacon returning true means only that the user agent queued the data.FIXED — fetch(..., {keepalive: true}), which also survives unload and exposes the response, so only a real 2xx confirms. Sealed batches are persisted and replayed by the next document with the same ids; if the first send actually landed, the replay is harmless because of A2 and N8.
N17`views UInt64` in an `AggregatingMergeTree` does not aggregate. The engine combines rows by merging aggregate states; a plain integer carries no instruction for how. Two inserts touching the same (site_id, hour, path) — the normal case — left whichever value won, not the sum. Pageviews would have been under-reported forever, plausibly, with no error.FIXED — views SimpleAggregateFunction(sum, UInt64); sessions keeps the full AggregateFunction(uniq) because distinct-counting cannot be summed. signups_daily was already correct for a reason now written down, so nobody "fixes" it into the same shape: SummingMergeTree sums plain columns by definition.
N18The queue lease was shorter than the drain it protects. A 10-minute visibility timeout against a 15-minute wall clock, with the worker draining to ~minute 14: a message pulled at minute 2 became eligible for redelivery while the invocation holding it was still running. Dedup protects correctness, so this is waste rather than corruption — but it is waste in exactly the window the design exists to keep short, and it makes duplicate metrics noisy enough to hide a real problem.FIXED — VISIBILITY_TIMEOUT_MS = 25 min, with assertLeaseOutlastsDrain() refusing before pulling anything if the invariant is violated.
N19Scrubbing before URL-decoding is a trivial bypass. ?utm_campaign=travis%40example.com survived round 2 untouched while the literal form was redacted — the parser scrubbed the encoded text, in which there is no @ to find.FIXED — decode (bounded, repeated until stable, so %2540 does not buy another layer) then redact. Also `journey_id` is now shape-bounded: C7 is open, nothing verifies issuance, so V1 accepts only our own jny_ format and drops anything else rather than admitting arbitrary strings into the column.
N20Vendor session/identity was wrong in both vendors. Amplitude got hashToInt(session_id) — a valid integer that meant nothing, since Amplitude defines session_id as the session start time in ms. PostHog got e_session_id, a property it has never heard of, so E's events took no part in session aggregation or replay correlation. And $set_once does not establish PostHog's identity relationship.FIXED — one canonical UUIDv7 session id, two correct derivations: PostHog $session_id = the UUID; Amplitude session_id = the ms timestamp read out of it. identity_linked now emits a PostHog `$identify` with `$anon_distinct_id`, ordered before the event it derives from.

`session_id` is now validated as a UUIDv7 at ingest, not merely produced as one by the SDK. If the vendor mapping requires the shape, accepting anything else means knowingly shipping broken data to two vendors.

6.2 The conceptual improvement inside N15 — E does not rewrite history

An anonymous pricing_viewed stays anonymous forever. That is what actually happened, and backfilling user_id onto it corrupts the epistemic state of a historical event to make a join easier.

anon_abc ── identity_linked ──► principal_xyz

The link is its own fact, with its own timestamp and its own linked_anonymous_id. Analytics can say "this earlier anonymous event belongs to the journey that later became principal_xyz" without claiming we knew who they were at the time.

This is also the shape the eventual Super projection needs, since a projection has to be able to state what was known when — and it is the same distinction the Cloud lane draws in R27 between a presented and an authenticated claim.

6.3 The pattern, now four rounds running

The defect keeps being in the thing built to prevent the previous defect.

  • A9 — the budget guard whose fixed reserve exceeded a 30-second budget.

  • N11/N12 — a ReDoS in the redactor, and a redactor that ate the attribution data it protects.

  • N13 — turning on async_insert would have silently un-done A2 on an older server. That

is why it ships with a version floor rather than a comment.

  • N16 — sendBeacon reopening the durable-acceptance hole N1 had just closed, one layer

down, in the same round.

Every round has now found at least one of these, and three of the four were found by the battery rather than by reading. That is the argument for the battery, and it is the reason to keep writing falsifiers for the fix and not only for the original bug.

6.4 Still open — unchanged, and deliberately not expanded

  • C7 cross-domain journey tokens (deferred by ruling; journey_id is shape-bounded until then)

  • §10/§16 ClickHouse prices — unverified; the pricing page is client-rendered

  • Retention TTL — a privacy decision that must equal the number the privacy page publishes

  • `INSERT_CONCURRENCY` — needs npm run bench:live

6.5 What only a real ClickHouse Cloud instance can answer

Round 3 is the end of what fakes can decide. These need the first staging deployment:

async-insert + dedup behaviour on SharedMergeTree, at the real service version
the materialized views, including the N17 fix under multi-insert merges
cold-start latency and actual scale-to-zero behaviour
insert concurrency (bench:live)
part counts and merge pressure per 2-hour flush
compressed bytes per event
active minutes per day  ->  the cost model's only real input

The prototype is instrumented for every one of them: the flush snapshot already publishes dedup_window, dedup_window_source, clickhouse_version, async_insert_dedup_supported, insert_concurrency, visibility_timeout_ms, block counts and durations — so the first staging run produces measurements rather than requiring new code to produce them.

7. Round 4 — the platform boundary, and idempotency across time

Travis relayed a review of the round-3 prototype which independently reran the battery (150/150) and raised eight findings, retracting round 3's claim that "fakes are finished." That retraction was correct. Two of the eight are demonstrable on this machine for nothing, and both would otherwise have been discovered by paying for a staging deployment.

Verifying the eight produced four more (N29–N32) and one correction to the review itself (N26). Every one of the four is the same shape round 3 named and then walked into again.

7.1 The findings

#FindingStatus
N21The first real Cloudflare pull would have thrown, on every run, forever. The adapter read typeof m.body === 'string' ? JSON.parse(m.body) : m.body, which reads as defensive and handles neither case. Cloudflare documents the pull body as base64-encoded for the json and bytes content types, and json is the default for any Worker after the 2024-03-18 compatibility date — which E is. So m.body is a base64 string for every message, JSON.parse throws SyntaxError on the first character, the flush records pull_failed, and the queue fills to retention while the dashboard says the pipeline is merely unhealthy. Round 3 also discarded `attempts`, `id`, `timestamp_ms` and `metadata` — and attempts is the only input N22's repair needs.FIXED — packages/e-schema/queue-wire.mjs decodes per metadata['CF-Content-Type'], refuses v8 by name, and preserves the whole envelope.
N22"A crash after a confirmed insert is safe because it dedupes" was true only for a retry that arrives SOON. Round 3's guard asked will this batch alone emit more blocks than the window holds? — always "no" at ≤25 events per message. The question that decides correctness is will this batch's token still be remembered when Cloudflare redelivers? The dedup log is a rolling global history; a token is evicted when either bound passes. Cloudflare is explicitly at-least-once.FIXED — two parts, neither sufficient alone: N31 bounds the redelivery horizon in time, and an existence probe gated on attempts > 1 asks the table rather than trusting Keeper. The Keeper window is now an optimisation, not a proof obligation.
N23The prerequisites were checked and then ignored. Round 3 read the window, read the version, appended an error string when the version was too old — and drained anyway. That is observability after corruption.FIXED — the drain refuses before the first pull if the version is not confirmed at or above the floor, if the window could not be read, or if N31's horizon invariant fails. A pull is the irreversible step; the Queue is what makes failing closed affordable.
N24A 15-minute credential frozen into a 24-hour retry. N15 froze the identity assertion into the sealed batch; N16 persisted sealed batches for 24 h. Composed: an authenticated batch that waits 20 minutes replays with an assertion that expired 5 minutes ago, 401s, and repeats until it is dropped. The batch cannot be re-signed — that is what N15 forbids.FIXED — the TTL now covers the pending horizon, and the credential is re-described as what it is: an analytics attestation with no product authority, carrying scp: e-analytics. See §7.3 on why the prose about key custody was also wrong.
N25Withdrawal erased the copy and kept the original. Round 3 cleared the queue, pending batches and storage — everything written down — and left anonymous_id, session_id, identity_assertion and journey_id live in memory. Deny → re-grant in one document recovered the same visitor. The SPA case (a banner toggled without navigation) is the normal one.FIXED — withdrawal is an identity boundary, like logout(). New ids are minted immediately and stay memory-only until analytics is permitted again.
N26The review argued the floor should be 26.1. Keeping 26.2 — and the reasoning matters more than the number. See §7.2.CORRECTED, floor unchanged
N27One vendor's outage duplicated into the other. Ack-if-both-succeeded on a shared queue meant an Amplitude outage retried the message and re-sent to PostHog every time — and round 2's own N8 establishes that Amplitude's insert_id makes its retries clean while PostHog's dedup is a four-tuple, eventual, and documented as not guaranteed. The duplicates landed on the vendor least able to absorb them, caused by the outage of the vendor best able to.FIXED — e-events-posthog and e-events-amplitude, one consumer each, batch.queue selects the vendor. Retries are isolated per destination.
N28A flag shipped `true` inside a comment arguing for `false`. Round 3 wrote "nothing verifies issuance, this is not a security control, C7 is deferred" and shipped E_JOURNEY_IDS_ENABLED = true. Separately, properties was bounded by size but not by schema, so any event could carry any 64 key names into a JSON column that materialises discovered paths into physical subcolumns.FIXED — journey ids off until C7 issues one; a per-event property registry beside vocabulary.mjs. Unknown keys are dropped and counted, not rejected: refusing the event to punish one key loses the funnel to protect the column.
N29E never turned deduplication on. Round 3 set async_insert: 1 and passed a dedup token, and stopped — because dedup "is the default". It is the default for synchronous inserts. ClickHouse's 26.2 changelog: "Deduplication is now enabled by default for all inserts. Previously it was off for async inserts and materialized views, but on for sync inserts." Below 26.2 the token was accepted and ignored. This is N4's own lesson — never hard-code a provider default — violated inside the fix for N13: round 3 read the window from the server and assumed the switch.FIXED — deduplicate_insert plus the legacy pair plus deduplicate_blocks_in_dependent_materialized_views, stated explicitly.
N30N4's protocol was reading a setting that does not govern E's inserts. ClickHouse keeps separate dedup bookkeeping for async inserts. Round 3 read replicated_deduplication_window — the sync one — while every insert is async. The number in the dashboard was real, was read from the server, and described a mechanism this pipeline does not use. A setting name is not a type, so nothing connected N13's change to N4's reader.FIXED — both families are read, and the active one is selected by async_insert rather than by whichever name got typed first. The snapshot publishes which family it read.
N31Three rounds counted blocks; nobody read the other bound. replicated_deduplication_window_seconds defaults to 3600 — one hour, against a two-hour flush cadence. The async variant is 604 800 (7 days). Had async_insert ever been reverted — which N13's own error message offers as the remedy for an old server — every token would have expired an hour before the flush that could have used it. The suggested fallback was a silent-duplication switch.FIXED — queue retention < dedup seconds is asserted before the first pull. Retention is declared at 4 days, not the 14-day maximum: 14 would be double the dedup memory, and "use the maximum" is the obvious safe-looking choice that breaks it. Note the direction reverses — for blocks the conservative declaration is smaller, for seconds it is a larger horizon and a smaller assumed memory.
N32The `batch_id` column was never populated. Found by writing the falsifier for N22's fix. events_v1 declares batch_id UUID and three rounds of prose are narrated around it — but every one of those statements is about the token, which is passed as an insert setting. normalizeEvent() emits no batch_id; the flush inserts batch.events verbatim; the column took the all-zeros default on every row, silently, because nothing reads it. What it breaks is every question the table can be asked about a batch — N22's probe first of all, which would have returned 0 for a batch demonstrably present and inserted it again. A fix for silent duplication that silently duplicates.FIXED — stamped in insertBatchIdempotent, which already takes batchId for the token, so a caller cannot insert a batch without saying which batch it is. Plus a bloom-filter index, since the probe is a point lookup on a column unrelated to the sort key.

The round-3 fixture is why N32 survived. aRow() minted a random batch_id per row, so every row looked correctly stamped and no test could see that nothing in the pipeline stamps it. The fixture now omits the field, exactly as normalizeEvent() does.

7.2 N26 — where the review was wrong, and it is the same shape as everything else

The review argued the floor should be 26.1, citing ClickHouse's 26.1 release note: deduplication "now works end-to-end for asynchronous inserts and their dependent materialized views."

That note is accurate and the conclusion does not follow, because capability and default are different events:

26.1   the capability lands   — async+MV dedup is made to WORK
26.2   the default flips      — "enabled by default for all inserts. Previously it
                                 was off for async inserts and materialized views"
26.3   async inserts become enabled by default

Lowering the floor to 26.1 would have admitted servers where the mechanism exists and is switched off — which is A2, re-opened by the fix for N26. Since round 3 set no dedup switch at all (N29), 26.1 would have deduplicated nothing.

With N29's settings now explicit, 26.1 would in fact behave. The floor stays at 26.2 anyway, because a floor that depends on remembering to send three legacy setting names is a floor resting on a comment — and E targets ClickHouse Cloud, which is past both.

This is worth recording plainly: the pattern reached the reviewer. A2 was nearly re-opened by the correction to a finding about A2. That is now the sixth instance.

7.3 The authority split HMAC does not provide

Round 2 wrote: "the signing key belongs to the auth boundary, and only the ingest Worker holds the verification key." With HMAC-SHA256 that sentence describes something that does not exist. The verification key is the signing key, so an ingest Worker able to verify an assertion is equally able to mint one for any principal on any site. There is no issuer/verifier split — only a shared secret in two places.

That is an acceptable V1 position (ingest and auth are the same trust domain) and it must be stated as what it is. Claiming a separation the cryptography does not provide is N9's defect — writing "FIXED" for something half-shipped — in a place where the consequence is an authority bug.

The real boundary is now scope: scp: e-analytics, checked at verify. A product API must refuse a token carrying it; E refuses one without it. Asymmetric signing is the upgrade that would make the custody claim true, and the verify path already takes the key as a parameter.

7.4 The pattern, now six rounds running

The defect keeps being in the thing built to prevent the previous defect.

  • A9 — the budget guard whose fixed reserve exceeded a 30-second budget

  • N11/N12 — a ReDoS in the redactor, and a redactor that ate the attribution data it protects

  • N13 — async_insert would have silently un-done A2 on an older server

  • N16 — sendBeacon reopening the hole N1 had just closed, in the same round

  • N29/N30 — N13's change moved which setting governs; N4's read-don't-assume protocol kept reading the old one, and nobody turned the mechanism on at all

  • N32 — found by writing the falsifier for N22's fix, and it would have made that fix duplicate

  • N26 — the proposed correction to a finding about A2 would have re-opened A2

Four of the seven were found by the battery rather than by reading. Write the falsifier for the fix. Round 4 did, and it produced N32.

7.5 What round 4 deliberately did NOT do

No website, no DNS, no ClickHouse account, no deploy. The review's framing was right: close the provider wire contract and cross-time idempotency locally first, so staging money is spent measuring rather than on bugs already provable here.

7.6 Still open

Unchanged from §6.4, plus:

  • C7 cross-domain journey tokens — now the reason journey_id is off, not merely bounded

  • §10/§16 ClickHouse prices — still unverified; the pricing page is client-rendered

  • Retention TTL — a privacy decision that must equal the number the privacy page publishes

  • `INSERT_CONCURRENCY` — needs npm run bench:live

  • The `batch_id` bloom filter's granularity — 1 is a guess biased toward the point lookup; it is a real index with a real cost and staging should measure it

  • N24's TTL is a judgement, not a measurement. A day-long analytics attestation is defensible only because it authorises nothing. If E ever gains an authority, this number is the first thing to revisit.

  • §36 Q12/Q13 — scale-to-zero and active-minutes still need a deployment

Unchanged from §6.5, with two additions the round-4 findings created:

that `deduplicate_insert` is accepted (not silently ignored) at the service version

8. Round 5 — acceptance atomicity, and deployed-configuration truth

The round-4 review reran the battery and got 186/187, against a saved log claiming 187/187, and caught the §1 header still saying 150. Both were real: one non-hermetic test, and a stale count in the document about claim discipline. It then raised nine findings, all nine of which reproduce.

8.1 The findings

#FindingStatus
N33The battery stopped being hermetic. test/round4.test.mjs called the real vendor Worker, which called deliver() with its default fetchImpl = fetch — so an ACK/retry assertion made a live request to https://us.i.posthog.com/batch/ with the fake key 'ph'. It passed here 3/3 and failed on the reviewer's machine 3/3, from identical code. The seam already existed one layer down and the Worker did not thread it through: a seam below the layer under test is not a seam.FIXED — env.FETCH through the Worker, and test/no-net.mjs replaces the global fetch with a throwing stub for the whole battery via --import. Not a convention; enforced.
N34BLOCKER. The probe could not run under the credentials this design specifies. The DDL grants e_ingest INSERT + SELECT(received_at), and ClickHouse SELECT privileges are column-scoped. SELECT count() ... WHERE batch_id = ? is a permission error under exactly those grants — which round 4 caught, turned into null, and inserted through. The mechanism was present in every test and absent in production, the worst of the two arrangements.FIXED — GRANT SELECT(batch_id, received_at), still two non-PII columns, and assertProbeCapability() runs before the first pull so the grant cannot silently regress.
N35BLOCKER. `attempts > 1` is not "this batch is a duplicate." It answers did Cloudflare redeliver this message, a strict subset. The ingest Worker's own partial fanout produced the counterexample: canonical send OK, Amplitude send fails, 503, browser retries the same batch_id — a second message in the already-successful canonical queue, both with `attempts = 1`. Reproduced: A rows = 2, probe calls = 0.FIXED — presence is asked for every pulled microbatch, as one grouped query per pull against the bloom filter round 4 added. Idempotency no longer depends on where the duplicate came from.
N36The cumulative window guard raced. Round 4 checked blocks_cumulative and incremented it after the await, so at INSERT_CONCURRENCY = 8 all eight workers passed one budget. Reproduced against the shipped code: window 2, blocks_cumulative 9, errors: [] — it reported the right reason for stopping while having written 4.5× the budget it enforces. Its falsifier passed because it was written with concurrency: 1, the one configuration under which the guard holds.FIXED — reserved synchronously, no suspension point between check and reserve; the reservation is returned on failure.
N37N4's protocol was applied to one side of the invariant only. queue retention < dedup seconds read the right-hand side from the server and supplied the left from a constant — and nothing in the repository sets that value on the queue either. 4 days is Cloudflare's current default, so it was right by luck. The maximum is 14 days, double the 7-day dedup memory, one dashboard field away.FIXED — readQueueRetention() reads the deployed value; an unreadable retention refuses the drain rather than falling back; the snapshot records which key answered.
N38N24's fix did not compose either. The TTL runs from mint, the pending horizon from seal. A tab open 23 hours seals a batch with ~1 hour of usable retry against a 24-hour window. Round 4 turned "always broken" into "usually fine" — harder to notice, no more correct, and the same defect one layer along.FIXED — the invariant is now exp − sealed_at ≥ PENDING_MAX_AGE_MS, checked at seal. An assertion that cannot survive the horizon is not frozen; the batch seals anonymously and the drop is counted. The event is never lost — only the identity label, and E does not rewrite history anyway (N15).
N39A missing vendor secret was treated as successful delivery and permanently ACKed. {ok: true, skipped: true} was defensible when one queue fanned out to two vendors. With N27's dedicated queues it became a data-loss path: one forgotten `wrangler secret put` silently discards that vendor's entire stream while every invocation looks healthy.FIXED — a queue that delivered a message requires its vendor to be configured; otherwise retry() and a logged error. A deliberate disable means not producing to the queue at all.
N40The two vendor queues were not configured alike. TOML array-of-tables: keys belong to the entry above them, so PostHog inherited platform defaults and had no DLQ — Cloudflare retries three times and then permanently deletes. N27 exists to give the vendors independent failure domains and gave them different data-loss behaviour. Staging had no DLQ on either. A visual diff reads as symmetric; the semantics are not.FIXED — both consumers configured explicitly, separate -dlq queues per vendor (a shared one destroys N27's "queue name identifies one vendor" invariant), staging included.
N41The size limit was bypassable and the fallback unbounded. There is an early Content-Length check — the review's "applied after the entire request has already been materialized" is slightly stronger than the code — but ?? '0' means an absent header passes, and Content-Length is absent under chunked encoding. Past that gate, await request.text() materialises whatever arrives, against a 100 MB platform ceiling and 128 MB of Worker memory.FIXED — readBounded() counts bytes off the stream, stops one byte past the limit, and cancels.

8.2 What 202 Accepted means — the architectural change

The review's last point was the most important and it is right.

Round 4 awaited all three queue writes and returned 503 if any failed, treating the fanout as atomic. It is not, and pretending it is put the cost on the wrong leg:

     ClickHouse queue  OK
     PostHog queue     OK
     Amplitude queue   FAILS
           ↓
         503  ->  the browser resubmits CANONICAL history
           ↓
     a second message in the already-successful canonical queue   [this IS N35]
     and a second delivery to PostHog, whose dedup is eventual
       and documented as NOT GUARANTEED                            [N8]

So a transient Amplitude enqueue problem manufactured a canonical duplicate and a visible vendor duplicate, in the vendor least able to absorb one.

202 now means exactly one thing: the canonical event is durably accepted.

This does not weaken N1, it makes N1 precise. N1's finding was that 202 must not mean "we parsed it"; it still must mean a durable boundary was crossed. What N1 never answered is which boundary, and the architecture already answers it — ClickHouse is the source of truth, the vendors are lenses, and a lens can be rebuilt from the source while the source cannot be rebuilt from a lens. A canonical failure is still 503 with retry_with_same_batch_id. A vendor enqueue failure is reported in the 202 body as vendor_enqueue_failed and reconciled downstream — never by asking the browser to resend history it has already been told was accepted.

8.3 The pattern moved

Rounds 1–4: the defect is in the thing built to prevent the previous defect. That still holds — N35 is inside N22's fix, N36 inside N22's other fix, N38 inside N24's fix, N39 inside N27's fix.

But round 5's other half is new, and it is worth separating:

rounds 1-4    a guarantee failed when composed with adjacent CODE
round 5       a guarantee failed when composed with adjacent CONFIGURATION
                  a column grant          N34
                  a queue retention       N37
                  a vendor secret         N39
                  a dead letter queue     N40
                  a Worker's fetch seam   N33

No amount of reading the source catches those, because the source is not where the fact lives. That is the argument for scripts/check-queue-config.mjs and for assertProbeCapability(): the things that decide correctness must be read from the system that enforces them, on both sides of every invariant that spans two providers. N4 said this about ClickHouse in round 2. It took until round 5 to apply it symmetrically.

And one thing no falsifier could have caught: the header of this document claimed 150 while the battery ran 187. The count is now derived from a live run by the bundle script.

8.4 What round 5 deliberately did NOT do

No website, no DNS, no ClickHouse account, no deploy. Strictly N33–N41 plus the 202 change.

8.5 Still open

  • C7 cross-domain journey tokens — the reason journey_id is off

  • §10/§16 ClickHouse prices — unverified; the pricing page is client-rendered

  • Retention TTL — a privacy decision that must equal the number the privacy page publishes

  • `INSERT_CONCURRENCY` — needs npm run bench:live

  • The exact Cloudflare queue-API JSON key for retention. queue-config.mjs tries three

documented spellings and publishes which answered, because there is no account to check against. The first staging run settles it in one line.

  • The `batch_id` bloom filter's granularity and real selectivity under the always-on probe. N35

made this a per-pull query on every flush rather than a rare one, so its cost is now on the hot path and is unmeasured.

  • `assertionOutlivesPendingHorizon()` reads an unverified payload. Correct here — the SDK has no

key and N3 forbids it being authoritative — but it means a malformed assertion seals anonymously rather than being rejected. That is the safe direction; it is still a judgement.

  • The N39 rule assumes a vendor queue implies a configured vendor. Disabling a vendor now means

removing the producer binding and the queue. Nothing enforces that pairing yet.

8.6 What only a real deployment can answer

Unchanged from §7.7, plus what round 5 added:

the real Cloudflare queue-API key and shape for message retention          [N37]
that GRANT SELECT(batch_id, received_at) is sufficient for the probe       [N34]
the bloom filter's selectivity under a per-pull IN(...) of up to 100 ids   [N35]
the cost of that probe in the flush's active-minutes budget               [N35]
that `deduplicate_insert` is accepted, not silently ignored                [N29]
the ACTUAL replicated_deduplication_window_*_for_async_inserts on Cloud    [N30]
async-insert + dedup on SharedMergeTree at the real service version
the materialized views, including N17 under multi-insert merges
cold start / scale-to-zero, insert concurrency, part pressure, compression
active minutes per day  ->  the cost model's only real input

scripts/check-queue-config.mjs answers the first tranche read-only, without spending anything, the moment credentials exist.

9. Round 6 — canonical batch identity, and fanout truth

The round-5 review ran the shipped battery independently, got 216/216, agreed the 202 ruling was correct, and then found seven more composition defects by reading the fixes. All seven verified against the shipped code. Verifying them produced three more of our own — one of which (N50) answers the experiment the review asked for, and answers it in the opposite direction to the question.

Battery: 259 falsifiers, 0 failing. 43 new, one per finding plus its witness.

9.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N42HIGHvendor_enqueue_failed was produced, transmitted, and discarded by res.ok; nothing durable ever recorded the gap, and "reconciled from ClickHouse" named no mechanism
N43HIGHthe fallback route derived the site from a constant, so every site's events were filed under e
N44MEDa same-pull duplicate reserved a block budget and continued without returning it
N45HIGHa row COUNT was standing in for a batch's content identity — same batch_id, different events, second batch ACKed into oblivion
N46HIGHidentity_linked could seal with its assertion dropped: a canonical fact asserting a link to nobody
N47MEDattempts was persisted and lastAttemptAt was not, so a reload restored the retry count and erased the backoff
N48LOW/MEDevery rejection message said UUIDv7; every check was isUuid. Stale 202 semantics in both wrangler files
N49HIGHours — and the fallback route destroyed all authenticated traffic, not just misfiled it
N50HIGHours — insert deduplication is scoped per partition, and E's partition key is stamped per attempt
N51MEDours — a count mismatch was read as a torn write when it is equally a vocabulary deploy, and that reading halts every later flush

9.2 N49 — the composition underneath N43

N43 is that the cross-origin route answered site_id = "e" for every caller. Composed with N3 it is worse than misfiling.

verifyAssertion(token, secret, expectedAudience) binds an assertion to one site, and expectedAudience is the site derived from the route. On the fallback route that was the constant e. So an assertion minted for a person on computedriven.com carries aud: "computedriven", meets a route that has decided the site is e, and fails:

401  bad_identity_assertion / wrong_audience

on every authenticated batch. 401 is not 2xx, so the SDK never confirms — the batch is retried from this document and every later one until the 24-hour horizon drops it. Anonymous traffic was misfiled; logged-in traffic was destroyed, after consuming the entire retry budget.

Two correct mechanisms, composed. N3 binds identity to a site; N43 derives the site from config. Together they reject exactly the traffic identity exists for.

The repair: site identity on that route comes from a server-issued site key in the path (/v1/sites/<site_key>/events), resolved against a server-side map. Origin is a CORS control and touches nothing else. The key is an identifier, not a credential — it ships in browser JavaScript. What it buys over Origin is that we issue it, resolve it, and can revoke it; calling it "authenticated" would be the N9 defect.

9.3 N45 — and why the fingerprint has to be minted by the SDK

The review's proposal was (site_id, batch_id, batch_fingerprint). That is right. The part it did not specify is where the fingerprint is computed, and computing it in the wrong place converts this fix into N51.

Ingest sees the accepted subset, not the batch, and what validation accepts is a function of the deployed vocabulary — §9 invites retiring event names, and N28 built the property registry that makes such changes routine. A fingerprint recomputed at ingest would therefore differ between an original and a retry that straddles a deploy, and the retry would read as an identity conflict.

The browser's sealed set is immutable (N15) and is already what batch_id names, so the fingerprint is minted once, at seal, by the SDK, carried unchanged, and copied — never recomputed — by ingest. FNV-1a 128 rather than SHA-256 because #seal() is synchronous and making it async would put a suspension point between "read the queue" and "empty the queue", which is N36 one layer down.

It is an accident-and-confusion check, not a signature. The question a digest cannot answer — "can I make my batch look like somebody else's?" — is answered by scoping: presence is keyed on site_id too, and site_id comes from the route, so a caller can only ever collide with itself.

9.4 N50 — THE EXPERIMENT, ANSWERED THE OTHER WAY ROUND

The review asked whether the always-on presence probe (N35) has made N31 (retention < dedup seconds) and N36 (the cumulative block budget) redundant as correctness gates rather than diagnostics. Answering it turned up a third bound nobody had read, in ClickHouse's own documentation of the feature:

deduplication "applies per partition: if the two queries write rows to different partitions, both survive."

E partitions by toYYYYMM(received_at) — A3, and correctly, because a browser's clock must not carve the storage layout. But `received_at` is stamped by the ingest Worker per ATTEMPT, so it is a property of the attempt, not of the batch. The pending horizon is twenty-four hours:

23:50, 31 Aug   attempt 1 accepted   received_at -> partition 202608
00:10,  1 Sep   attempt 2 accepted   received_at -> partition 202609
                same batch_id, same token, DIFFERENT PARTITIONS
                -> "both survive"

Twelve times a year there is a 24-hour window in which the token is not evictable but inapplicable — and no guard in the flush measures it, because every guard measures when the token expires, not whether it applies.

So the experiment's answer is not "the window gates can relax". It is:

PRIMARY, and at times the ONLY mechanism
    the presence probe  —  queries the TABLE, which has no partition predicate,
                           so it sees rows wherever they landed

RACE PROTECTION ONLY
    the dedup token     —  free, immediate, and structurally unable to hold
                           across a partition boundary

WINDOW GATES (N31/N36)
    bound the durability of a mechanism that is sometimes not running.
    They cannot be the proof of anything.

Two falsifiers establish which mechanism holds the property: with the token switched off entirely (dedupWindowSeconds: 0) the probe alone prevents the duplicate; with the probe removed the token alone does not.

THE CONCLUSION IS RECORDED, NOT ENACTED. Demoting N31 from a refusal to a diagnostic trades a hard stop for a metric, and in this tree that is an R-number and Travis's call — not a side effect of a test passing. The gates still refuse, and a falsifier pins that behaviour so it cannot drift while the question is open.

Open for ruling:

  1. Do N31/N36 become diagnostics, with the probe (N34/N35) as the sole hard gate?

  2. Should received_at be frozen at first acceptance and carried on retry, so a batch has one

partition for its whole life? That would restore the token across month boundaries — and it re-opens A3, because the value would then come from a client-held field.

9.5 The pattern, now seven rounds running

Round 5 named the move from composed with adjacent CODE to composed with adjacent CONFIGURATION. Round 6 is a third thing, and it is the one that generalises furthest:

AN IDENTITY WAS STANDING IN FOR A DIFFERENT IDENTITY, AND THE SUBSTITUTION WAS INVISIBLE BECAUSE BOTH SIDES WERE REAL VALUES.

  • a row count standing in for a batch's content identity (N45)

  • a route constant standing in for the site (N43), and therefore for the audience (N49)

  • an event named identity_linked standing in for a link (N46)

  • a table-wide token standing in for a per-partition one (N50)

  • a torn write standing in for a vocabulary deploy (N51)

Each substitution type-checks, reads correctly, and produces a plausible number. None of them fails loudly, and four of the five are silent data defects rather than errors.

And the defect kept being in the thing built to prevent the previous defect, for the seventh round: N44 is N36's reservation missing from one exit of N36's own loop; N45 is the presence proof N35 introduced; N46 is N38's repair; N49 is inside N43's fix; N51 is inside N35's quarantine.

Two defects were found in round 6's own work while writing its falsifiers, which is the ALWAYS WRITE THE FALSIFIER FOR THE FIX rule paying out again:

  • The new FakeClickHouse probe regex used ([^)]*\)[^)]*) for the tuple list and could not cross

more than two ) characters. It matched a pull of one batch and a pull of two, and silently failed on three or more — a non-matching probe query falls through and returns nothing, which reads downstream as no batch is present. The entire N45/N35 closure would have tested green while being unreachable in every realistic pull.

  • A ${partition} ${token} template picked up a literal NUL byte in place of the space, so the

fake stored tokens under one separator and looked them up under another. It also made grep silent on those exact lines, which is how it survived two rounds of reading.

9.6 What round 6 deliberately did NOT do

Unchanged from §8.4, and now explicitly: no E website, no Super chat, no cross-domain journeys, no portfolio rollout. C7 stays deferred and E_JOURNEY_IDS_ENABLED stays false.

9.7 Still open

Everything in §8.5, minus what round 6 closed, plus:

  • The two rulings in §9.4.

  • `vendor_repair_v1` has a writer and no reader. The repair record is durable and the

reconciliation job that consumes WHERE repaired_at IS NULL does not exist. That is deliberate — the record had to exist before anything could be built on it — but until the job ships, E can say which events a vendor is missing and cannot yet re-deliver them.

  • The site-key map has no issuance path. E_SITE_KEYS is a secret an operator writes by hand.

Fine for one site; it needs a real registry before "general fallback for external integrations" is a true description.

  • FNV-1a 128 is not collision-resistant against a motivated caller. Scoping makes that

uninteresting today (a caller can only collide with itself, on its own site). It stops being uninteresting the moment a site key is shared across tenants.

  • `batch_fingerprint` adds 32 bytes per row and a groupUniqArray to the hot-path probe.

Neither is measured.

9.8 What only a real deployment can answer

Unchanged from §8.6, plus:

the real cost of groupUniqArray(2) + tuple IN over the bloom filter      [N45]
whether SharedMergeTree's dedup is partition-scoped in the same way      [N50]
   — the docs say per partition; ClickHouse Cloud substitutes the engine,
     and round 4 already learned that substitution changes the answer
the vendor_repair_v1 write's share of the flush's active minutes         [N42]

This is the boundary. Round 6 was the last round the fakes can decide — and round 3 said that too, and was wrong, so the correct form is the one §7.7 uses: these specific questions now need a real instance, and the local list is empty for the first time since round 1.

10. Round 7 — canonical identity, and serialized acceptance

The round-6 review unpacked the bundle, read the implementation rather than the findings, ran the battery independently (259/259), confirmed N49/N50/N51, and disputed one sentence: that the local list was empty. It was not. Four more — and two of them are inside round 6's own repairs.

Battery: 288 falsifiers, 0 failing. 29 new.

10.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N52HIGHthe "content fingerprint" hashed only the event IDs, so N45's own defect survived one level down — and round 6's test for it varied the ids, the single field the function read
N53MED/HIGHN48 diagnosed event_id and batch_id in writing and then fixed only batch_id
N54BLOCKERpresence is check-then-act and nothing serialized it across drainers — while N50 had just removed the mechanism silently covering that
N55HIGHschema_version: 1 froze nothing; a deploy changed what a shipped version means, and round 6's N51 accommodated the consequence instead of removing the cause

10.2 The pattern, now eight rounds running

Round 5's was composed with adjacent configuration. Round 6's was an identity stood in for a different identity. Round 7's is narrower and worse:

THE REPAIR NAMED THE RIGHT PROPERTY AND IMPLEMENTED A WEAKER ONE.

  • N45 said "a row count is not a content identity" and hashed only the ids

  • N48 said "event_id and batch_id — the two ids the whole closure keys on" and fixed one

  • N51 said "the fingerprint is immune to what ingest decides" and used that immunity to **ACK a

divergence between the source and its lenses**

Each comment is an accurate description of a property the code does not have. Reading the code for what it claims confirms it; only running the claim falsifies it. That is why the reviewer's move — read the implementation, not the findings — found four things six rounds of reading findings did not.

Round 7 committed the same defect twice more, both caught by its own battery: schemaFor() replaced a typed Set membership test with a hasOwnProperty lookup and started accepting the string "1"; and a comment about -0 said the opposite of the (correct) line beneath it.

10.3 N52 — and why the fingerprint sorts events but not property arrays

The digest now covers the full sealed events plus the frozen identity assertion, through a deterministic canonicalEncode (recursive key sort, type tags, length prefixes — so distinct structures cannot share an encoding, which plain concatenation allows).

The first draft encoded the events array in its given order, on the reasoning that array order is content. That broke closure 2b — "a reordered redelivery still deduplicates end to end" — and the break was the finding, not a fixture to update. The token derives from the fingerprint and identifies a block; blocks are built by orderDeterministically(), which sorts rows by event_id so a redelivery in a different order produces byte-identical blocks. So:

fingerprint order-SENSITIVE  +  blocks order-INSENSITIVE
   -> two byte-identical block sets carrying DIFFERENT tokens
   -> dedup silently misses

The rule the two layers must share:

The fingerprint must be invariant under exactly the transformations the insert path is invariant under — no more, and no less.

The insert path sorts the event list by event_id and touches nothing else. So the fingerprint sorts the event list by event_id and touches nothing else; arrays nested in properties keep their order, because nothing downstream reorders them.

-0 normalises to 0 for a related reason: #restorePending() re-derives a fingerprint from storage that has been through JSON.stringify, where -0 is already "0". Distinguishing them would make a restored batch stop being itself because the page reloaded.

Still FNV-1a 128, still explicitly not a signature. Scoping by site_id means a caller can only collide with itself on its own site — an argument that fails the moment one site key is shared across tenants, which is when SHA-256 becomes required rather than preferable.

10.4 N54 — and the honest limit of the fence

EFlushCoordinator, a Durable Object holding one lease: {epoch, holder, acquired_at, expires_at}. Acquired after the dedup prerequisites and before the first pull (N23: a pull is the irreversible step), released on every exit, only by the current epoch. KV was rejected — eventual consistency means both readers can see "no lease" in exactly the contended case.

Cloudflare's warning against a global high-throughput singleton is respected and worth stating precisely: this object sees two requests per flush at a two-hour cadence. No event, no batch and no ClickHouse I/O passes through it, and nothing is held inside blockConcurrencyWhile() across a network call.

What the fence does and does not guarantee. A true fence would have the store reject a stale epoch; ClickHouse has no such facility. So the fence is a check the holder makes on itself (now + margin < expires_at, before each pull and each insert), which bounds the overlap to one in-flight insert rather than to zero. Without a lease the window is the whole drain — up to fifteen minutes of two drainers probing and inserting freely. Within the residual window the dedup token still covers the same-partition case, which is every case except the month boundary. If that residual is ever judged too large, the next step is a claim row in ClickHouse keyed on the batch identity — not a longer margin.

The fence is checked before the deadline. Both stop the drain and both are safe, so the order only decides what the snapshot says — and under the shipped numbers the deadline (14 min) always arrives first, making a second-place fence unreachable in exactly the case it exists for. Reporting time_budget there would hide the only fact an operator needs. The battery caught this: fence_stops: 0.

10.5 N55 — the lens could outrun the source

schema_version was a label, not a version. The rules it named lived in module-level globals, so a deploy changed what {"schema_version": 1} means. Round 7's own N53 did exactly that, making v1 reject UUIDv4 event ids it had previously accepted — a correct fix that silently redefined a shipped version.

The consequence round 6 accommodated rather than removed:

sealed batch [A, B]
attempt 1, pre-deploy    v1 rejects B   -> ClickHouse [A],  vendors [A]   (202 lost)
deploy                   B joins v1
attempt 2, SAME batch    v1 accepts B   -> vendors [A, B]
                                        -> flush: 1 row, fingerprint MATCHES
                                        -> N51 ACKs it, B never reaches ClickHouse

CLICKHOUSE   A            POSTHOG / AMPLITUDE   A, B

A semantic event in a lens and not in the source — the inverse of the sentence the architecture rests on. schemas.mjs freezes each version's vocabulary, property registry, acceptance-gating limits and id formats, with a digest the battery asserts so an edit fails npm test naming the two legal moves: mint v2, or use a new event name. The limits are in the schema because freezing the vocabulary and leaving PROPERTIES_MAX_BYTES tunable leaves the same divergence reachable by a different knob; OCCURRED_AT_MAX_SKEW_* are deliberately not, because they clamp rather than reject (A3) and so change a value, never a count.

With drift impossible, N51's accommodation is withdrawn. A count mismatch is unexplainable again, and unexplainable is a quarantine (N23).

10.6 The two N50 rulings

1. `received_at` stays server-stamped per attempt — ruled NO on freezing it. Carrying it back on a retry would make the storage partition depend on a browser-held field, which is A3 walked back in. The epistemic split is kept: occurred_at is the client's claim, received_at is our observation of this accepted attempt. N50's consequence is absorbed by making the probe primary and serializing acceptance, not by making a server fact client-supplied.

2. N31/N36 → diagnostics: agreed in principle, NOT YET ENACTED. The reviewer ruled "yes, but only after N54 is closed with strong single-drainer coordination." N54 is closed against fakes. The coordinator has never run on Cloudflare, no Durable Object has ever been created, and "acceptance is serialized" currently rests on a class in this repository behaving the way its own test says.

Round 3 said "this is the end of what fakes can decide" and rounds 4, 5, 6 and 7 each falsified it for free. So the demotion waits for the first staging flush to show a real lease acquired, refused and released. A falsifier pins the current behaviour until then.

10.7 Still open

  • The N31/N36 demotion, gated on a real lease (above).

  • `vendor_repair_v1` has a writer and no reader — unchanged from §9.7.

  • Site-key issuance is manual; E_SITE_KEYS is a secret written by hand.

  • FNV-1a 128 is not collision-resistant. Adequate while site_id scoping means a caller can only

  • The fence's residual window is one insert. Bounded, stated, unmeasured.

  • The DO adds a call to the flush's critical path and its latency is unmeasured.

  • `batch_fingerprint` adds 32 bytes per row plus a groupUniqArray on the hot-path probe.

10.8 What only a real deployment can answer

Unchanged from §9.8, plus:

that EFlushCoordinator's lease behaves under REAL overlapping cron invocations   [N54]
the DO's acquire/release latency inside the flush's active-minutes budget         [N54]
