11. Round 8 — acceptance evidence, and the outbox lifecycle

The round-7 review read the implementation rather than the findings, reran the battery independently (288/288), agreed with both N50 rulings — and then invoked round 7's own exception to "then staging": nine more, each reproduced locally before it was reported. Round 8 reproduced all nine again from scratch before touching anything, and found a tenth while checking whether one of the proposed repairs was safe.

Battery: 338 falsifiers, 0 failing. 50 new.

11.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N56BLOCKERthe content fingerprint was still a client claim — validated for shape and copied, so N45 was bypassable without finding a hash collision at all
N57HIGHthe encoding was injective over JS values, and the fingerprint is about wire values, which are a different set — in two unrelated ways
N58BLOCKERa missing E_FLUSH_COORDINATOR binding meant "coordination unnecessary" rather than "coordination unprovable", so a wrangler typo silently reopened N54
N59HIGHlogout() deleted the durable outbox while a send was still in flight
N60HIGHa late consent grant left a persisted outbox unread until the 24-hour rule dropped it
N61HIGHundefined from a transport meant "durably accepted"
N62MED/HIGHthe vendor repair log inherited N50's partition hole, and its comment said it did not
N63HIGH (cost)an empty queue woke ClickHouse three times, and the test denying it was counting inserts
N64MED/HIGHthe lease's expiry was decided using the clock of the caller asking to take it
N65HIGHfound locally — the canonical queue had no dead letter queue and Cloudflare's default retry limit of 3, while the disposable lenses had 5 and a DLQ each

11.2 The pattern, now nine rounds running

Round 7's was the repair named the right property and implemented a weaker one. Round 8's is one layer out from that:

THE EVIDENCE WAS ASSERTED BY THE PARTY IT WAS EVIDENCE ABOUT.

  • the fingerprint was minted by the sender and never checked (N56)

  • the delivery acknowledgement was whatever the transport returned, and returning nothing counted (N61)

  • the lease's expiry was decided with the clock of the caller asking to take it (N64)

Three different layers, one shape: a proof supplied by the thing it was supposed to constrain. Each was individually defensible when written — the SDK does mint the fingerprint, the transport does know whether it succeeded, the Worker does know the time — and the defence is the error. Knowing a fact is not the same as being the right party to attest it.

N57 and N63 are the round's other half and rhyme differently: both are claims that were true of one representation and false of the one that matters. "Injective" was true of JS strings and false of the bytes. "An empty queue does not keep ClickHouse awake" was true of inserts and false of queries.

11.3 N57 — one finding, two defects, and only one of them is a mismatch

The review filed these together and they behave differently, so they are separated here.

(a) Lone surrogates are an injectivity failure, not a browser/server mismatch. Every unpaired UTF-16 surrogate encodes to the same UTF-8 bytes — measured, "\uD800" and "\uD801" both give ef bf bd — so canonicalEncode distinguished them and fnv1a128Hex could not.

But JSON.stringify escapes a lone surrogate to the six ASCII characters \ud800 (well-formed JSON.stringify, ES2019), so it survives a real UTF-8 wire round trip intact — also measured. Both ends therefore computed the same colliding value. Nothing disagreed; two distinct wire batches simply shared one identity. That is what makes it load-bearing for N56: the verification can be bypassed without touching the hash, by mutating one lone surrogate to another.

Fixed by normalising, not refusing. A string truncated across a surrogate pair — s.slice(0, 100) through an emoji — is the ordinary way a real analytics property acquires one, and refusing would drop genuine events for a defect of ours. Normalising before the fingerprint makes the encoding injective over the values that can actually cross the wire, which is the set the fingerprint is about.

(b) `[undefined]` and sparse holes ARE a mismatch. JSON.stringify([undefined]) is "[null]", and so is a hole. Round 7's encoder gave array-undefined its own tag, so the browser fingerprinted a value the server can only ever receive as something else.

Latent until now, because #restorePending() prefers the stored fingerprint. N56 makes it fatal: ingest recomputes from the parsed body, gets a different digest, and refuses the batch on every attempt until the horizon drops it. So this is not "also worth fixing" alongside N56 — shipping N56 without it converts a silent mis-fingerprint into silent event loss. They ship together.

The rule both halves serve:

The fingerprint describes the JSON value that crosses the network, not the JavaScript object that produced it.

toWireValue() is where a JS value becomes a wire value, at track(), before anything is queued. It mirrors JSON.stringify exactly where that is lossy but harmless, and refuses where JSON.stringify would invent a value we could not explain — a NaN that becomes null is a measurement that becomes an absence, which is A3 walked back in.

The battery found two real bugs in this repair. Array.prototype.map skips holes, so the first draft of the sparse-hole guard could not see the one case it was written for, and the first draft of toWireValue returned a still-sparse array that merely looked right under JSON.stringify. Both are indexed loops now. The round's own pattern, one level in: a guard that named the right property and used a primitive that could not implement it.

11.4 N63 — and where round 8 declines to do what the review proposed

The review's diagnosis is exactly right, including that the test denying it was counting insertCalls while three ClickHouse queries ran underneath. Measured before: queue depth 0 | pulls 1 | inserts 0 | QUERIES 3. After: queries 0.

Its correction to N23 is also right, and worth restating because round 4 got it slightly too strong: a pull only leases a message; the ACK is what destroys it. An unacked message returns after the visibility timeout, which N18 already guarantees outlasts the drain.

But the repair as proposed would have introduced data loss, and this is the one place round 8 departs from the review. "A pull is reversible" is true once and false repeatedly. Cloudflare counts delivery attempts, and at the retry limit — default 3 — a message with no dead letter queue is, in Cloudflare's own words, deleted permanently. So preflighting after a non-empty pull spends one retry per cron cycle during a ClickHouse outage, and at a two-hour cadence that destroys the canonical backlog six hours into an outage which the old ordering survived for the full four-day retention. That is a straight reversal of §28.14.

Checking whether that hazard was real is what produced N65. The repair therefore ships as two halves that are only safe together:

empty pull    -> free. no message, so no attempt to count.       <- all of the cost benefit
non-empty pull -> costs one attempt if the preflight then refuses <- needs N65

N63 and N65 ship together or neither ships.

11.5 N65 — the finding the review's list does not contain

cd-e-vendors/wrangler.toml gives PostHog and Amplitude max_retries = 5 and a dedicated dead letter queue each. The canonical queue has a pull consumer, so it has no [[queues.consumers]] block in any wrangler.toml, and nothing else set either value:

e-events-posthog      max_retries 5    DLQ e-events-posthog-dlq
e-events-amplitude    max_retries 5    DLQ e-events-amplitude-dlq
e-events-clickhouse   max_retries 3    DLQ NONE            <-- the canonical one

The queue carrying the canonical history — the one whose integrity eight rounds exist to protect, the one the vendor tables are explicitly lenses onto — was the only one that silently destroyed its contents, at the lowest retry budget of the three. The architecture's priority order, implemented backwards. Nobody decided that; nobody decided anything, and the default decided.

scripts/check-queue-config.mjs missed it because its stated invariant list says "each vendor queue has its own dead letter queue" — N40's scope, faithfully implemented, never widened when the canonical queue's own durability became load-bearing.

And the fix has an honest limit that lands somewhere interesting. Pinning max_retries at Cloudflare's ceiling of 100 does not hold at every cadence:

120 min -> needs  48 attempts    ok
 60 min -> needs  96             ok
 58 min -> needs 100             ok, exactly at the ceiling
 30 min -> needs 192             THE RETRY BUDGET BECOMES BINDING

That boundary is the same one-hour interval A9 found, arrived at independently two rounds and one review apart: below an hour the flush gets 30 seconds of CPU instead of 15 minutes (A9) and the retry budget starts expiring the backlog before retention does (N65). Neither is visible in the cron expression, and brief §6 actively invites tightening it. assertRetryBudgetCoversRetention() refuses rather than degrades.

11.6 N59 — why preserving the outbox across a logout is the safe direction

There was one forget(), it deleted all three storage keys, and both logout() and consent withdrawal called it. But they are asking different questions:

CONSENT WITHDRAWAL   "stop holding my data"        -> erase EVERYTHING, sealed work included
LOGOUT               "different person from now"   -> rotate the IDENTITY; the sealed work is
                                                      already the other person's and is owed to them

N16 spent a round making sealed batches outlive the document, and logout() deleted the durable copy of one still in flight — reproduced: in-memory pending 1, persistent pending absent. A navigation in that window loses the batch outright, which is the exact failure N16 exists to prevent, opened by the call most likely to be followed by a navigation.

Splitting it is safe because of N15: every pending batch carries the assertion frozen when it was sealed, so a batch retried after logout stays attributed to the person who generated it and cannot become the next person's. The falsifier asserts that directly.

11.7 N61 — and why "backward compatibility" was the wrong reason

The comment defending undefined → confirmed cited round 5's contract. E has never been deployed. There is no shipped transport to be compatible with, so what was being preserved was compatibility with the prototype's own fakes — the cheapest possible moment to break it, defended as though it were the most expensive.

The failure mode is now a duplicate delivery rather than a lost batch, and duplicates are what eight rounds of idempotency work exist to absorb: same batch_id, same event_ids, same fingerprint, so the presence probe drops it. Loss is the one failure the architecture cannot repair.

  • No new architecture. Every finding was closed in place; nothing was re-designed.

  • `vendor_repair_v1` still has no reader. N62 gives it a stable identity and a probe before the

reader exists, which is cheaper than fixing the reader, but the reader is still not written.

  • FNV-1a 128 is unchanged. Still not collision-resistant, still adequate only while site_id

scoping means a caller can collide only with itself. SHA-256 remains the upgrade.

  • Nothing was deployed. No Cloudflare resource was created and no money was spent.

11.10 What only a real deployment can answer

Unchanged from §10.8, plus:

that a Cloudflare pull WITHOUT an ack really does increment `attempts`      [N63/N65]
whether an EMPTY pull leaves the attempt counters untouched, as reasoned     [N63]
that max_retries and dead_letter_queue can be set on an http_pull consumer   [N65]
the real skew between the Worker's clock and the DO's, now measured          [N64]

The threshold. Round 7's was "N52–N55 closed, the two rulings made, then staging", and the review declined to cross it on the strength of nine locally reproduced holes. Round 8 closes all ten and adds no architecture. The remaining questions in §11.10 are all provider questions — every one of them is a fact about Cloudflare or ClickHouse that no fake can settle, which is a different category from the last eight rounds, where the fakes kept finding real defects for free.

Round 8's own view: this is the staging round. But note what N65 did to that confidence — it was found not by reviewing the design but by checking whether a proposed repair was safe, in a file nobody had reason to reopen. The honest statement is that the fakes have stopped finding architecture defects and have not stopped finding configuration ones, and staging is where configuration becomes observable.

12. Round 9 — harness truth, and event identity

The round-8 review unpacked the bundle, read the implementation, and reran the battery — and got 337/338 where the bundle recorded 338/338. Same code, same machine, one day later.

That single discrepancy is the round. Four more findings followed from reading the round-8 repairs, and the reviewer's constraint was explicit: close these, change no architecture, then create the staging resources. Round 9 does exactly that and adds nothing.

Battery: 360 falsifiers, 0 failing — at today's date AND five years on. 22 new.

12.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N66MED/HIGHthe battery, asserted hermetic since N33, verified assertions against the wall clock — so a green run decayed on a timer
N67HIGHthe deployed-config checker — the thing round 8 said staging needs — crashed with a ReferenceError on its healthy path
N68HIGHevent_id had a stronger contract in the vendor adapter than in E itself; nothing enforced uniqueness, and Amplitude dedups on it
N69MED/HIGHbatch_version named a version and selected nothing; ingest overwrote whatever arrived with a hard-coded 1
N70LOWthe generated bundle carried a Round-8 banner over a header still saying "rounds 2–7" and "288 falsifiers"

12.2 The pattern, now ten rounds running

Round 8's was the evidence was asserted by the party it was evidence about. Round 9's is narrower, and it is about us rather than about the system:

THE THINGS THAT CHECK THE SYSTEM WERE NOT THEMSELVES CHECKED.

  • the battery had a guard against the network and none against the clock (N66)

  • the deployment gate had never been executed (N67)

  • the bundle generator derived its test count from a live run and its **narrative from a hand-typed

header** (N70)

Every one of these is this project's own discipline — executable, not prose; derived, not typed — applied rigorously to the product and not at all to the tooling that judges it. Nine rounds were spent making the system prove its claims while the harness making those claims was exempt.

N68 is the exception, and the only genuine semantic question in the round.

12.3 N66 — a green battery with a fuse in it

verifyAssertion defaulted nowSeconds to Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000). Every test caller passed an explicit time; the one caller that did not was the ingest Worker, which is the only caller that matters. The fixture mints at NOW = 1_787_500_000_000 with a ~24h15m lifetime, so:

2026-08-23   338 / 338          the bundle was generated here
2026-08-24   337 / 338          same code, same machine, different date

test/no-net.mjs closes the network because an ambient dependency is one a test must not silently acquire. The clock is the same kind of dependency and had no such guard.

The fix is structural, not a corrected default. nowSeconds is now required — a missing one is a TypeError, deliberately not an AssertionError, so a caller's bug cannot read as a rejected credential. The Worker takes one observation, requestNow(env), and uses it for both assertion expiry and received_at; the falsifier asserts the clock is read exactly once per request. That buys a second thing worth having: an assertion can no longer expire between being verified and the batch it authorised being stamped.

And the guard is now permanent. test/time-travel.mjs shifts Date.now(), new Date() and the zero-argument Date constructor five years forward and the whole battery runs again — a shift rather than a freeze, so every interval is preserved and only an absolute-date dependency can break. npm run test:all runs both, and the bundle generator refuses to build unless both are green.

The guard was verified against the defect rather than assumed to catch it. With round 8's code restored exactly, on a simulated 2026-08-23:

DEFECTIVE code, real date         338 / 338     <- what round 8 shipped
DEFECTIVE code, +5y time travel   337 / 338     <- what would have caught it, the same day

12.4 N67 — the deployment gate had never been run

The canonical-queue block read found.settings?.message_retention_period, and found is declared with const inside the vendor loop forty lines below. Reproduced against a mocked healthy account:

ReferenceError: found is not defined
scripts/check-queue-config.mjs:203

Two things make this worse than an ordinary typo. First, it crashes only when the account is healthy — the block runs only if the canonical queue exists, so a missing queue would have returned earlier and survived. Second, round 9 wrote it in round 8 and could not have noticed, because the script short-circuits without credentials and there were none.

A deployment gate with no test is prose that looks like code — the argument rounds 5 through 8 kept making about the system, aimed at the wrong file.

checkQueueConfig(queues) is now a pure exported function — API payload in, verdict out — with the CLI a thin wrapper that fetches, prints and exits. Nine falsifiers drive it across a healthy account and every N65 misconfiguration. The value it should have used was already in scope: seconds, the number extractRetentionSeconds() had already normalised across the provider's spellings. And when that is null the script has already concluded retention is unprovable, so substituting the declared constant would be N37 exactly — comparing a fact against a wish and reporting the wish as checked. It refuses instead.

The reviewer also confirmed externally that Cloudflare's API exposes dead_letter_queue and settings.max_retries on an http_pull consumer, which removes one of §11.10's open provider questions: N65's provisioning is not asking for a feature that does not exist.

12.5 N68 — the ruling, and the half that staging has to settle

THE RULING: within a site, `event_id` identifies one immutable logical event. Canonical event identity is `(site_id, event_id)`.

It needed to be made because the vendor adapter had already made it by implication and E had not. normalizeEvent runs per event with no cross-event state, so a batch could carry one id twice with different payloads — reproduced, ok: true, accepted: 2, both surviving.

The consequence is lens-vs-source again, from the opposite direction to N55. Amplitude's adapter maps insert_id: event.event_id, and Amplitude ignores a later event with the same insert_id for seven days:

CLICKHOUSE (source)        AMPLITUDE (lens)
X  page_viewed             X  page_viewed
X  pricing_viewed          (dropped as a duplicate)

The whole batch is refused, not the second event dropped. Two differing payloads claiming one identity is an integrity conflict, not an invalid optional property — and N56's fingerprint covers both, so a partial accept would produce a message whose contents no longer match the identity it was admitted under. A malformed id remains a per-event rejection, because two events with no identity are not the same identity twice.

What this does not close, stated plainly: the same `event_id` in two different batches. Canonical idempotency is batch-scoped (N35/N45), so both are accepted today. The reviewer is right that UUIDv7 improbability is not an argument here, because this is a publicly writable endpoint. The options are a per-event presence query, a compact identity ledger, or something else — and the hot path is the reason not to choose blind: a two-hour drain can hold thousands of events where the batch probe handles at most ~100 identities.

So it is a staging measurement, and there is a falsifier pinning the current behaviour so the gap cannot be mistaken for a closed one and so whichever mechanism is chosen has a test to turn red first.

12.6 N69 — N55, one layer up

batch_version: 1 was on every request, never read, and then overwritten by a hard-coded 1 in the output message. Measured: missing → 1, 0 → 1, 2 → 1, 999 → 1, "1" → 1.

That is precisely N55's content — a version label that does not select semantics makes a compatibility claim nothing enforces — at the envelope layer that N55 did not reach. It is latent only while one version exists: the moment a v2 envelope ships, a v2 sender talking to a v1 deployment is accepted, silently reinterpreted, and relabelled v1, and N56's fingerprint would not catch it because the fingerprint covers the events and the assertion, not the envelope.

Numeric 1 or refused. No coercion — the string "1" fails, because round 7 already had schemaFor() start accepting "1" through a lookup that did not check the type. The constant now lives in one place that both the SDK and ingest import, so they cannot drift.

12.7 What round 9 deliberately did NOT do

Exactly what the reviewer scoped, and nothing else:

  • No architecture changes. Workers, Queues and ClickHouse are untouched.

  • No rate limiter. The brief calls for one and the prototype still has none. Agreed as a

public-production gate, not a staging gate — staging exists to learn provider behaviour before E is exposed broadly.

  • No cross-batch event-identity mechanism. Ruled, pinned, deferred to staging measurement (§12.5).

  • Nothing deployed. No Cloudflare resource created; no money spent.

12.8 Still open

  • The N31/N36 demotion, gated on a real Durable Object lease.

  • Cross-batch `event_id` reuse (§12.5) — ruled, unenforced, pinned by a falsifier.

  • No rate limiting or bot controls — public-production gate.

  • `vendor_repair_v1` has a writer and no reader.

  • FNV-1a 128 is not collision-resistant — SHA-256 before one site key is shared across tenants.

  • Site-key issuance is manual.

  • N63's non-empty branch spends a delivery attempt on a refusal — bounded by N65, unmeasured.

  • `toWellFormed` is ES2024; the fallback is asserted equivalent but has never run on an old browser.

12.9 What only a real deployment can answer

active ClickHouse minutes per day under the two-hour cadence      THE COST QUESTION
whether EFlushCoordinator's lease behaves under real overlapping crons      [N54]
whether SharedMergeTree dedup is partition-scoped as documented             [N50]
that a pull WITHOUT an ack increments `attempts`, and an empty pull does not [N63/N65]

The threshold, and round 9 accepts the reviewer's line without amendment: N66–N70, then staging.

The remaining questions are now all provider questions or explicitly-deferred measurements. Round 8 said that too and was wrong by five — but the five were of a different kind: three were tooling defects in the harness rather than the system, one was a contract the vendor layer had already decided, and one was a document header. The system's design has survived nine rounds without a component being replaced. What is left is the thing no local phase can produce: whether two-hour buffering actually lets ClickHouse sleep enough to land in the $10–$30/month neighbourhood.

13. Round 10 — the vendor-repair race, and the fakes' own gaps

A patch, not a round, scoped exactly as the round-9 reviewer scoped it: close N71, clean two stale claims, stop. The reviewer independently reran both batteries (360/360 and the +5y run), confirmed the derived header now agrees with reality, and checked Cloudflare's current API docs against N65's provisioning — then found one real defect in N62's repair.

Reproducing it turned up a second, in the fakes.

Battery: 374 falsifiers, 0 failing — at today's date and five years on. 14 new.

13.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N71MED/HIGHN62's presence probe runs once per pull, and the repair path had no inFlight set — two copies of one repair in one pull both read "absent" and both inserted, into different partitions
N72LOW"hermetic against the clock" overstated what the time-shift battery proves
N73LOWthe prototype README was still at 288 falsifiers and a round-7 layout
N74HIGHfound locally — the fakes could neither partition a repair row nor answer the repair presence query, so both halves of N62 were untestable and one of them had never worked

13.2 N71 — the same TOCTOU, one scope smaller

Round 8 gave repairs a stable identity and a presence probe, and closed the case it was written for: the same repair re-detected in a later pull. It did not close two copies in one pull, because the probe runs once before the workers start and all eight then measure themselves against that one snapshot:

probe -> R absent
     worker A            worker B
     absent              absent
     INSERT R            INSERT R
     202608              202609      <- detected_at straddles a month

and the dedup token cannot span partitions, which is the whole of N50 and the whole reason N62 exists. Reproduced against the shipped flush: 2 rows, 2 partitions, `vendor_repairs_recorded: 2`, no errors.

The canonical path has had inFlight since N35 for exactly this shape. The repair path was given the probe and not the set, so N62 solved one half of a two-part problem and read as though it had solved both. It is N54's TOCTOU one scope smaller: N54 serialises across drainers, this serialises within one.

The twin is left unacked rather than made to wait — the same choice the canonical path makes (N44). Waiting would put one worker's progress on another's latency inside a budgeted window, and the queue already has a mechanism for "come back later". The next flush's probe then answers from the table definitively: measured, flush 1 writes one row and acks one message, flush 2 reports vendor_repairs_deduped: 1 and acks the twin. One logical repair, one row.

13.3 N74 — the fakes could not see the table they were vouching for

Found while building the N71 witness, and it is the larger finding.

First half — the partition key. partitionOf() read rows[0].received_at and nothing else. events_v1 partitions on received_at; vendor_repair_v1 partitions on detected_at, and a repair row has no received_at at all. Measured against the shipped fake:

partitionOf([{received_at: '2026-08-31T23:59Z'}])  ->  '202608'
partitionOf([{detected_at: '2026-08-31T23:59Z'}])  ->  'unpartitioned'
partitionOf([{detected_at: '2026-09-01T00:01Z'}])  ->  'unpartitioned'

So every repair row landed in one phantom bucket, the dedup token was effectively global for that table, and the exact hazard N62 exists to close was unrepresentable. Round 8 added a presence probe for a mechanism its own fakes modelled as unnecessary, and the tests passed either way.

It also masked N71. The first witness reported vendor_repairs_recorded: 2 with one row in the table — the flush really did insert twice and the fake collapsed them. A fake that hides a defect while printing the counter that proves it is worse than one that cannot see it.

Second half, and worse — the probe had no handler. classifyRepairPresence() issues a query the fake did not recognise, so it fell through to return []. An empty result is not "the query failed"; it is "none of these repairs are recorded" — the answer insert.mjs calls the most dangerous possible one in the comment directly above the function. So the probe reported ABSENT for every repair, forever, and N62's cross-pull closure had never detected anything. Witnessed end to end: a repair written by one flush was written again by the next.

Round 8's N62 tests passed presence in as a literal Set. They proved insertVendorRepair behaves correctly given a presence set and never proved the set is ever populated — two halves of one mechanism, each tested against a stub of the other.

This is round 6's own sentence, left true of a second table for two rounds:

A fake that cannot represent the mechanism's scope cannot falsify a claim about its scope.

partitionOf is table-aware now, from a map the battery asserts against ddl.sql; and an unrecognised query against events_v1 or vendor_repair_v1 throws rather than answering [], so a missing fake is loud.

13.4 N72 — the claim is now the size of the evidence

Round 9 called the battery "hermetic against the clock" by analogy with N33's network guard. The analogy overstates it, and in this project that is itself a finding: N9 is the rule that a claim must not exceed its evidence, and it was broken by the sentence describing the fix for the last time it was broken.

no-net.mjs removes the network. The time-shift harness does not remove the clock, and ambient reads remain on purpose — uuidv7's default, the SDK's default now, requestNow()'s fallback, and the coordinator's own clock, which N64 requires to be real. So the code was right and the sentence was wrong. What is proved:

The battery is invariant under a five-year wall-clock epoch shift.

What is not: that nothing reads ambient time (false), invariance under a clock running at a different rate, or one that moves backward mid-run. Those are worth having and are not what this is.

13.5 N73 — the count is removed, not corrected

The README said npm test # 288 falsifiers and listed test files up to round7.test.mjs, through two rounds. N70 fixed exactly this defect in `FINDINGS.md` and left the copy of it one directory down — N53's shape ("diagnosed two, fixed one"), applied to documents.

The number is not corrected. It is removed. FINDINGS.md's header is generated from a live run, so exactly one place in the repository states a count and nothing can disagree with it.

13.6 Still open — and this is the staging list now

  • Cross-batch `event_id` reuse (§12.5) — ruled, unenforced, pinned by a falsifier, mechanism to

be chosen on measured cost.

  • No rate limiting or bot controls — public-production gate, agreed.

  • `vendor_repair_v1` has a writer and no reader.

  • The N31/N36 demotion, gated on a real Durable Object lease.

  • FNV-1a 128 is not collision-resistant — SHA-256 before one site key is shared across tenants.

  • Site-key issuance is manual.

  • N63's non-empty branch spends a delivery attempt on a refusal — bounded by N65, unmeasured.

13.7 The staging constraint, accepted

First staging traffic is controlled and synthetic, not public. The reviewer's condition, and it follows directly from §13.6: cross-batch event identity is unenforced and there is no rate limiting, so an arbitrary caller could deliberately reuse ids against the very mechanism we are trying to measure.

staging SDK / synthetic sender  ->  staging ingest Worker  ->  real Queues
     ->  real Durable Object  ->  real ClickHouse Cloud Basic

13.8 What only a real deployment can answer

ACTIVE CLICKHOUSE MINUTES PER DAY under the two-hour cadence   <- the cost question
EFlushCoordinator's lease under real overlapping crons                      [N54]
whether SharedMergeTree dedup is partition-scoped as documented             [N50]
that an unacked pull increments `attempts`, and an empty pull does not [N63/N65]
Worker-to-Durable-Object clock skew, now measurable                         [N64]

Round 10 makes no architectural change and adds no mechanism. Ten rounds and 374 falsifiers have not replaced Workers, Queues, Durable Objects or ClickHouse.

One thing is worth stating plainly rather than as confidence. Round 8 said the remaining questions were all provider questions and was wrong by five; round 9 said it and was wrong by four. Both times the residue was in the harness rather than the system — the battery's clock, the deployment gate, the bundle header, and now the fakes themselves. That is a real pattern and it is nearly exhausted, because the fakes have now been audited against the DDL and made loud where they were silent. But the honest form of the claim is not "there is nothing left"; it is that what is left is no longer answerable here, which is a different sentence and the one that justifies staging.

14. Round 11 — the acceptance status, and configuration truth

The final pre-staging patch, scoped exactly as the round-10 reviewer scoped it: N75, N76, two stale comments, stop. The reviewer declined another adversarial architecture round and was right to — nothing here is a design question. Both findings were reproduced against the shipped code before being patched, and reproducing N76 turned up a third.

Battery: 396 falsifiers, 0 failing — at today's date and five years on. 22 new.

14.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N75HIGHthe protocol says 202 and browserTransport implemented res.ok, so 200/201/204/299 all released the batch — and the same Worker answers 200 on /health
N76HIGH (lens)a missing vendor binding was indistinguishable from a vendor deliberately turned off; and a stale E_EVENTS_VENDORS binding created a third delivery path to both vendors at once
N77HIGHfound locally — the consumer's unknown-queue fallback bypassed N39's missing-credential guard entirely and ACKed in silence
cleanupLOWthe ingest header and the batch_fingerprint DDL comment each described a superseded protocol

14.2 N75 — the protocol was written down three times and enforced a fourth way

Measured against the shipped transport:

HTTP 200 -> confirmed true      HTTP 299 -> confirmed true
HTTP 201 -> confirmed true      HTTP 300 -> confirmed false
HTTP 202 -> confirmed true      HTTP 503 -> confirmed false
HTTP 204 -> confirmed true

Five rounds went into making 202 mean one exact thing (N1, N5, N16, N48, N61). The comment directly above the defect even stated the intent correctly — "202 releases the batch" — sitting on top of res.ok, which releases it on a hundred statuses.

The witness was already deployed in the same file. /health answers 200 to a POST. Point the SDK endpoint at it — a plausible copy-paste, and exactly the sort of thing a staging config does by accident — and every batch is confirmed and deleted while nothing has crossed the canonical Queue boundary. That is the class of false acknowledgement N1, N16, N39 and N61 each closed one instance of, left open in the fifth place.

Why it survived ten rounds, and this is the part worth keeping. The battery had two transport tests. They were named:

'N2  browserTransport confirms only on a 2xx'
'N16 the transport no longer uses sendBeacon, and confirms only on a real 2xx'

and between them they exercised 202 and 503 — the two statuses on which res.ok and status === 202 give the same answer. A test named for a wider contract than it checks cannot fail when the code implements the wider contract. Both names now say 202, and the sweep that can actually tell the two rules apart is in round11.test.mjs.

The wording repair — the reviewer is right that the sentence was too narrow

202 is returned from two places, and only one of them is an acceptance:

202 = E HAS TERMINALLY HANDLED THIS BATCH.
      either  the canonical event is durably accepted
      or      it was suppressed by an authoritative privacy signal (Sec-GPC / DNT, N9)

      In BOTH cases the browser must not retry.
      EVERY other status leaves the batch pending.

The privacy branch returns 202 with accepted: 0 having deliberately stored nothing. Collapsing it into "durably accepted" would have the transport claiming a row exists for an event that was intentionally never written. Answering 204 there instead would be tidier prose and a worse protocol: the SDK would keep the batch and re-send it every session for 24 hours, against a user who asked not to be measured.

The value is now ACCEPTED_STATUS in e-schema/limits.mjs, imported by the side that produces it and the side that requires it, because N75 is those two sides keeping separate copies of one boundary. A falsifier asserts neither file contains a re-typed 202 in executable code.

14.3 N76 — absence meant two different things and nothing could tell them apart

canonical queue present, both vendor bindings absent:
    status                   202
    canonical messages       1
    vendor_enqueue_failed    []          <- nothing failed
    vendor_repair_recorded   false       <- so nothing to repair

Every counter reports health. PostHog receives nothing, forever. A Wrangler typo that drops the producer is observationally identical to a deployment that turned PostHog off on purpose.

This is N39's own ruling left standing on the other side of the boundary. N39 found that a missing secret must not look like a successful delivery, and fixed it in the consumer. Its rule — "a deliberate disable is expressed by not producing to the queue at all" — is sound only if something independent says the omission was deliberate. Nothing did. The producer went on inferring intent from a thing being missing.

So the repair is not a new mechanism; it is the missing input to the one N39 already assumed:

enabled + binding present   ->  enqueue
enabled + binding ABSENT    ->  vendor_enqueue_failed + a durable vendor_repair row
not enabled                 ->  do not enqueue, and report `vendors_disabled`
named but unknown           ->  `vendor_config_errors`. NOT a repair row.

An unknown name gets no repair record on purpose: a repair row means these events still need delivering, and nothing can ever deliver to a vendor with no adapter — the row would be permanently un-repairable, which is worse than the typo.

The round-5 ruling is preserved without amendment. A vendor configuration failure still never turns a canonical 202 into a 503. We record the lens gap; we do not ask the browser to resend canonical history over it.

The absent case is the whole design, so it is stated rather than defaulted. E_ENABLED_VENDORS unset means every known vendor is expected; "" means none, on purpose. Both are guesses and they fail in opposite directions: "none" restores this finding exactly (a deploy that forgot the line delivers to nobody and looks healthy), while "all" makes a forgotten line produce a loud false alarm an operator fixes in one edit. Over-reporting is recoverable; silence is not — which is N61's sentence, applied to configuration.

E_EVENTS_VENDORS is deleted, not deprecated. Measured, a stale binding alongside the two dedicated ones produced a third delivery path: canonical 1, posthog 1, amplitude 1, legacy 1 — the same events delivered to each vendor twice, through a queue whose consumer then had to guess which vendor it meant. Nothing is deployed; this is the cheapest moment there will ever be to close the contract, and round 8 already made this exact argument (N61: "E HAS NEVER BEEN DEPLOYED, so the compatibility being preserved was with the prototype's own fakes").

14.4 N77 — the fallback bypassed the guard that exists for this

Found while reproducing N76, and it is the sharpest of the three. Three states, one message each, measured against the shipped consumer:

queue               credentials   fetches   result
e-events-posthog    absent        0         retry + loud console.error   <- N39 works
e-events-vendors    absent        0         ACK, IN SILENCE              <- N39 BYPASSED
e-events-vendors    present       2         ACK, both vendors called     <- N27 resurrected

The middle row is N39's own defect, reached through the fallback N39 shipped beside. deliver() reports a missing credential as {ok: true, skipped: true}. The guard that catches that reads const leg = vendor ? legs[vendor] : null — so with no vendor identified there is no leg to inspect, relevant.every(l => l.ok) is true because a skipped leg reports ok, and the message is acked. One forgotten secret plus one queue rename discards that vendor's stream permanently while every invocation looks healthy. That is, word for word, the sentence N39 exists to make false.

The bottom row rebuilds N27's shared failure domain from a queue rename: an Amplitude outage retries the message and re-sends to PostHog, whose dedup is eventual and documented as not guaranteed.

And the battery was pinning it. §28.33-36 asserted:

assert.equal(acked.length, 1, 'no vendors configured -> nothing to fail -> ack');

against a batch with no queue name, written in round 2 — the round before N39 — which is why N39 never noticed that its own guard had a hole beside it. The test has been rewritten to assert what §28.33-36 is actually about: a failure retries, a success acks.

No fallback now. An unrecognised queue is refused, logged, and retried rather than acked, so it reaches the DLQ if the misconfiguration persists. Failing closed is safe because batch.queue is not optional — Cloudflare's MessageBatch declares readonly queue: string (Queues JavaScript API docs, checked 2026-08-24), so the only way to reach the refusal in production is a queue this consumer genuinely does not serve.

14.5 The pattern, and it is one pattern

A DEFAULT THAT ANSWERS A QUESTION IT WAS NEVER ASKED.

res.ok              answers "did something 2xx"          asked: "did E accept this"
.filter(b => b)     answers "is there a binding"         asked: "should this vendor be reachable"
?? null -> both     answers "which vendors exist"        asked: "which vendor is THIS message for"

Each is correct-looking. Each is wider than the question. And each fails in the direction that loses data rather than the direction that duplicates it — which is the distinction rounds 1 through 10 spent themselves on (N1, N16, N39, N61), found three more times in the places nothing had yet pointed at.

14.6 One falsifier did not falsify, and that is a finding about the method

Every round-11 witness was run against a deliberately reverted copy of the code it names. One did not fail there on the first attempt.

The /health witness read unconfirmedEvents immediately after await c.flush(). But flush() is deliberately synchronous from the caller's view — §28.8b, so navigation never waits on it — and returns a summary rather than the delivery promise. So the await resolves before the transport settles, and the assertion measured the pre-settlement state: 1 under the fix and 1 under the defect. It passed against both.

That is N75's own sin — an assertion that cannot distinguish the two behaviours it is named for — committed inside the test written to close N75. It waits on onDelivery now, which is the moment the batch's fate is actually decided, and it fails against the reverted copy.

A falsifier that has not been run against the defect it names is a claim, not evidence.

  • Cross-batch `event_id` reuse (§12.5) — ruled, unenforced, pinned by a falsifier.

  • No rate limiting or bot controls — public-production gate.

  • `vendor_repair_v1` has a writer and no reader.

  • The N31/N36 demotion, gated on a real Durable Object lease.

  • FNV-1a 128 is not collision-resistant — SHA-256 before one site key is shared across tenants.

  • Site-key issuance is manual.

  • N63's non-empty branch spends a delivery attempt on a refusal — bounded by N65, unmeasured.

Round 11 adds nothing to this list and removes nothing from it. It is a protocol/configuration patch, not an architecture round.

that an unacked pull increments `attempts`, and an empty pull does not [N63/N65]
Worker-to-Durable-Object clock skew, now measurable                         [N64]
what a per-event identity check costs on a full two-hour drain              [N68]
cold start, merge pressure, compression, bloom-filter/probe cost

Eleven rounds and 396 falsifiers have not replaced Workers, Queues, Durable Objects or ClickHouse. The round-10 reviewer's conclusion stands and round 11 does not soften it: continuing to simulate Cloudflare now has lower information value than turning the real staging plane on, with controlled synthetic traffic (§13.7).

15. Round 12 — the deployment description catches up with the code

The round-11 reviewer read the files as an actual --env staging deployment rather than as application code, declined another architecture round, and found three seams. One was a staging blocker. All three were reproduced against the shipped files before being patched.

Battery: 415 falsifiers, 0 failing — at today's date and five years on. 19 new.

15.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N78BLOCKERcd-e-flush's [env.staging] declared a name, a coordinator and a cron and nothing else — no vars, no KV — so a staging deploy would pull from accounts/undefined/queues/undefined
N79HIGHthe deployment gate hardcoded production queue names, so the one check standing between us and staging could not certify staging
N80MED/HIGHN77's "unknown queues fail closed" was a prefix rule, which trusted every hyphen suffix — including the dead letter queues
cleanupLOWpackage.json said "round 10" during round 11; cd-e-ingest/wrangler.toml kept the superseded one-line 202 claim

The pattern is not round 11's. Round 11's was a default that answers a question it was never asked. This one is:

THE APPLICATION SEMANTICS ARE MORE MATURE THAN THE DEPLOYMENT DESCRIPTION.

Eleven rounds hardened what the code does. Nothing had yet read the files that say which code runs where the way the deploy command reads them. Every finding here is in a .toml, a name, or a script, and none of them questions Workers, Queues, Durable Objects or ClickHouse.

15.2 N78 — a named environment inherits nothing that matters

Round 11 learned this rule one file over and wrote the reasoning into cd-e-ingest/wrangler.toml: Wrangler named environments do not inherit non-inheritable keys. Then it applied the rule to the file it was looking at and not to the others. Parsed directly:

top-level vars          present     staging vars           NONE
top-level E_SNAPSHOTS   present     staging E_SNAPSHOTS    NONE
top-level DO            present     staging DO             present

wrangler deploy --env staging would have produced a flush Worker whose pull URL formed as https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/undefined/queues/undefined/messages and whose ClickHouse endpoint formed as undefined/?query=.... The missing E_SNAPSHOTS is the quiet half: snapshot writing is deliberately optional in the flush, so the dashboard's data would simply never appear with nothing reporting a problem.

Audited all three configs rather than the one named, and cd-e-vendors had it too: [env.staging] declared no vars, so POSTHOG_HOST was absent. That one does not produce an undefined URL — adapters.mjs reads it as env.POSTHOG_HOST ?? 'https://us.i.posthog.com' — which is worse in a smaller way: a deployment that deliberately configured a different PostHog host (EU region, a proxy) would have staging silently post to the US endpoint with every leg reporting ok. A default standing in for a configured value is still a default.

Staging gets its own KV namespace, not production's. Sharing one would have a staging flush overwrite the live dashboard's single snapshot key with synthetic data, silently — the same "one shared thing, two failure domains" defect as N27, applied to the read side, and brief §26's rule.

`secrets.required` is now declared in all three configs. Listing required secrets in a comment is how E has described them for seven rounds and a comment cannot refuse a deploy. Wrangler validates the declared names at wrangler deploy and fails with the missing ones:

missing secret  ->  BAD:  deploy succeeds, the first cron finds out
                    GOOD: deployment itself refuses

which is N39 ("a missing secret must not look like a successful delivery") moved from first-message to deploy-time, the cheapest place there is. E_ASSERTION_SECRET earns this especially: absent, it does not fail closed on its own — every authenticated batch 401s and retries to the 24-hour horizon while anonymous traffic flows normally, which is N49's exact failure shape and invisible in aggregate volume.

Checked, rather than assumed: migrations and triggers are inheritable; vars, durable_objects, kv_namespaces, queues and secrets are not (Wrangler configuration docs, 2026-08-24). A check demanding that migrations be restated would be noise, and noise in a deployment gate is how a real finding gets scrolled past.

The battery can now read a wrangler.toml. The reviewer found N78 by parsing TOML; nothing in the battery had ever read one as configuration — round 11's registry test greps it for substrings, which answers does this string appear and not is this key declared under that table. There is a table-header scanner in test/wrangler-toml.mjs now, and the general check ("every worker restates every non-inheritable key in every environment it declares") runs against all three files. The scanner refuses the TOML constructs it cannot read rather than approximating them, because N74 is the finding that a fake which cannot represent the mechanism reports the claim as proven anyway.

15.3 N79 — the gate could only certify the deployment we were not making

Reproduced against a healthy mocked staging account — HTTP pull consumer, 4-day retention, max_retries 100, canonical DLQ, vendor DLQs, 25-minute visibility, everything correct:

FAIL  e-events-clickhouse does not exist
FAIL  e-events-amplitude does not exist
FAIL  e-events-posthog does not exist

Three failures on an account with nothing wrong with it. Not a provider uncertainty and not something staging would have taught us — locally decidable, and it is the first thing the staging sequence runs.

It is N67 again. That finding was "a deployment gate with no test is prose that looks like code", and round 9 gave this file falsifiers. Every one of them drove it at production names, so they proved the logic and could not notice the logic was pointed at the wrong account.

The environment is a parameter of the pure function now, defaulting to production so every round-9 falsifier keeps its meaning, and all six names derive from the grammar. The printed provisioning commands follow `--env` too — that is the quiet half. A staging preparation session that printed production wrangler queues create lines is one copy-paste from creating the production queues early, and a queue that exists is a queue this gate stops asking about, so that mistake is quieter than the missing check was.

An unknown --env is refused, not defaulted: --env staigng defaulting to production would report every staging queue missing and point an operator one step away from the fault.

15.4 N80 — "fails closed" was an open set

e-events-posthog-staging        -> posthog      <- intended
e-events-posthog-dlq            -> posthog      <- NOT intended
e-events-posthog-dlq-staging    -> posthog      <- NOT intended
e-events-posthog-typo           -> posthog      <- NOT intended
e-events-posthog-old            -> posthog      <- NOT intended
e-events-amplitude-dlq          -> amplitude    <- NOT intended

Round 11 stated the contract as "anything other than the queues this Worker serves → loud refusal + retry" and implemented name === stem || name.startsWith(stem + '-'), which is not that sentence — it is anything beginning with a vendor stem and a hyphen, an infinite set.

The dead letter queue is the case that matters. Attach cd-e-vendors to e-events-posthog-dlq by mistake — a plausible dashboard slip, and exactly what N40 created those queues for — and N77 was supposed to say "I do not serve this queue". It said "PostHog, carry on", re-delivering batches that had already exhausted their retry budget, forever, with no path out because a DLQ has no DLQ.

And the round-11 falsifier had the same hole it was testing for. It asserted vendorForQueue('e-events-posthogus') === null and called that "a near-miss name does not match", with a comment about the separator being required. Both the code and the test agreed on the one case that cannot distinguish a prefix rule from a closed set. That is N75's own finding — "a test named for a wider contract than it checks cannot fail when the code implements the wider contract" — committed in the round that named it, one file away, by the same hand.

Membership is generated, not parsed. packages/e-schema/queue-names.mjs owns a closed grammar (<base>[-dlq][-<environment>], environments a closed list); matchQueueName() constructs every valid name for a base and compares equality. Nothing inspects a suffix, so no suffix can be admitted by accident. A DLQ matches the grammar and is still refused, and the refusal now says which kind of not-ours it is — an operator who attached the consumer to a dead letter queue must not be sent hunting for a typo that is not there.

15.5 Still open — unchanged from §13.6

Round 12 adds nothing to the list and removes nothing from it. Cross-batch event_id reuse, rate limiting, vendor_repair_v1's missing reader, the N31/N36 demotion, FNV-1a's collision resistance, manual site-key issuance, and N63's refusal cost all stand exactly as §14.7 left them.

15.6 The staging sequence, and the first experiment

The reviewer's order, accepted without amendment:

create staging queues -> create staging DLQs -> configure the HTTP pull consumer
        -> npm run check:queues:staging   MUST BE GREEN
        -> create the staging KV -> deploy EFlushCoordinator
        -> deploy ingest / flush / vendors with --env staging
        -> set STAGING secrets (deploy now REFUSES without them, N78)
        -> controlled synthetic traffic ONLY -> force failures -> measure ClickHouse

The first experiment answers the original economic question and nothing else:

How many minutes per day does ClickHouse actually stay active when twelve two-hour windows are available — including cold start and post-insert background merge time?

Cross-batch event_id enforcement and rate limiting stay out of staging deliberately (§13.6). Those are reasons for controlled synthetic traffic, not reasons to keep Cloudflare imaginary.

Twelve rounds and 415 falsifiers have not replaced Workers, Queues, Durable Objects or ClickHouse. What is left is not answerable here.

16. Round 13 — falsifying the deployment procedure itself

The round-12 reviewer read the new staging instructions against the current Wrangler CLI and API and found four tooling defects. Two would have blocked the first staging setup. Every claim below was verified against the wrangler actually installed on this machine (4.115.0) rather than against documentation — including the failure text.

Battery: 435 falsifiers, 0 failing — at today's date and five years on. 20 new.

16.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N81BLOCKERsecrets.required + wrangler secret put is a bootstrap loop on a Worker that has never existed — deploy refuses, and secret put has nothing to put a secret on
N82BLOCKERthe generated HTTP-pull command used --max-retries, which is not an option on that command; the one line that sets N65's retry budget would not have executed
N83HIGHthe queue gate asserted "has a DLQ" rather than *"has the right DLQ"* — and printed the wrong name inside its own ok line
N84MEDthe queue inventory read page one of a paginated endpoint

The pattern, and it is worth stating plainly: the system has largely stopped failing review; the deployment procedure is what is being falsified now. That is the natural continuation of round 12 — round 12 made the deployment description match the code, and this round makes the deployment procedure match the tools that execute it. It is a good boundary to reach before the first deployment rather than after it.

16.2 N82 — a printed command is prose until something checks it

$ wrangler queues consumer http add fake-queue-xyz --max-retries 100
✘ [ERROR] Unknown arguments: max-retries, maxRetries

The flag is --message-retries. It fails at parse time rather than creating a consumer with the wrong setting, which is the better of the two failures and still a blocker: N65 is the finding that Cloudflare's default of 3 retries destroys the canonical backlog six hours into an outage the queue is retained four days for, and this command is the only place that number is ever set — N40 established that HTTP pull cannot be declared in a wrangler.toml at all.

The trap is real and worth naming, because the next person will be tempted to "fix" the checker instead: the API field is max_retries and the CLI flag is --message-retries. Both are correct for their own surface. The gate reads the API field and wrote the CLI flag, and the two being differently spelled is exactly how one became the other.

That string had been in the repository since round 5, inside the file whose entire purpose is "turn deployment truth into executable instructions". Nothing could catch it because a printed command is prose until something checks it — N67 aimed at the gate's output rather than at its logic. Commands are generated by functions now, every flag is checked against a surface transcribed from wrangler --help at a named version, and the builder refuses to return a command carrying an unverified flag rather than returning one and logging about it.

A first draft of the round-13 falsifier caught something I would have shipped: the gate's own explanation of N82 printed --max-retries three lines below a block of copy-pasteable commands. Being right about history does not make a bad flag safe to print next to good ones. The history is in the source and here; the terminal gets commands.

16.3 N81 — the documented sequence could not run

wrangler deploy --env staging       ->  refuses, required secret missing
wrangler secret put X --env staging ->  the Worker does not exist yet (API 10007)

Round 12 added secrets.required on purpose and it does exactly what it says. For a Worker that has never existed, that turns round 12's own instructions into a loop. Cloudflare carries this as workers-sdk issue #14258, closed against a fix to the error guidance rather than to the behaviour. The path that closes the loop is wrangler deploy --secrets-file <file>, which uploads the initial secrets with the first version.

The instructions were wrong only in the state we are about to enter. After the first version exists, secret put is the correct rotation command and always was.

The repair is not a corrected paragraph. N81 is an ordering defect and round 12 shipped the sequence as prose in §15.6; prose cannot be run, so an ordering defect in it is found by a careful reader or by an operator at 2am. scripts/staging-plan.mjs makes each step declare what must already exist and what it brings into existence, and a falsifier walks the plan from an empty account asserting nothing is ever required before something provides it. It would have caught N81 mechanically — and the falsifier demonstrates that by running round 12's order and watching the two steps require each other.

The ephemeral secret files are gitignored before any exists. The ordering is the point: the moment such a file is worth creating is a moment under deployment pressure, which is the worst moment to be deciding whether it is ignored.

16.4 N83 — "has a thing" is weaker than "has the right thing"

Reproduced against the shipped round-12 checker, with PostHog's staging queue wired to Amplitude's DLQ:

ok: true   problems: []
ok    e-events-posthog-staging has a dead letter queue (found e-events-amplitude-dlq-staging)

The gate printed the wrong name inside its own `ok` line. That is worse than not gathering the evidence: a reader scanning for FAIL sees a green run whose text contradicts it. Both vendors' failure domains terminate in one DLQ there — N27's shared failure domain rebuilt one layer down, in the place N40 built specifically to prevent it.

namesFor() had derived the expected pairing since round 12 and checkQueueConfig() dropped the field when destructuring. The check is positional now, and the two DLQs are additionally required to differ. A DLQ string is also weak evidence on its own: Cloudflare creates a named dead letter queue automatically if it does not exist when a consumer is configured, so seeing a name proves a name was typed, not that the intended topology exists.

16.5 N84 — the gate read page one

List Queues is paginated: per_page defaults to 20, maximum 100, and result_info.total_pages carries the rest. An E queue on page two reads as does not exist — nothing misconfigured, the verifier incomplete. That gets likelier as the account accumulates infrastructure that has nothing to do with E.

per_page is set to the documented maximum and every page is fetched — not one or the other. The maximum alone is a bet that the account stays under 100 queues; the loop alone is correct but pays five times the requests. The loop is bounded independently of total_pages, because a loop bounded only by a number the other side supplies is a loop the other side controls.

16.6 The toolchain, pinned without a dependency

The reviewer is right that the operator tooling is not conceptually zero-dependency: it rests on secrets.required, --secrets-file, the named-environment inheritance rules, and a specific command surface.

Adding wrangler as a devDependency would put a large tree behind a battery that currently needs none — npm test runs on a clean checkout, and that is worth keeping. The middle path: record the version, record the surface, check our commands against the surface in the battery, and check the ambient wrangler against the version at provisioning time. A mismatch is a printed note rather than a refusal, because a gate that refused to run on a version bump would be turned off, and a gate that is off catches nothing.

16.7 Still open — unchanged from §13.6

Round 13 adds nothing and removes nothing. Cross-batch event_id reuse, rate limiting, vendor_repair_v1's missing reader, the N31/N36 demotion, FNV-1a's collision resistance, manual site-key issuance, and N63's refusal cost all stand exactly as §14.7 left them.

16.8 The sequence, and the first measurement

npm run plan:staging prints it, order-checked, from zero resources:

queues + DLQs -> canonical HTTP pull consumer (--message-retries 100)
   -> check:queues:staging  MUST BE GREEN  -> staging KV -> real resource ids
   -> FIRST deploy each Worker WITH --secrets-file

The first thing wanted from that deployment is not a dashboard. It is this table, and the local battery cannot manufacture a single row of it:

MeasurementReal result

per-event identity probe projected cost?

Thirteen rounds and 435 falsifiers have still not produced a reason to replace Workers, Queues, Durable Objects or ClickHouse. Stop reviewing the imaginary staging environment and make it real.

17. Round 14 — staging bootstrap closure

The round-13 reviewer accepted the architecture for the fourteenth time, reran the battery independently (435/435, and 435/435 under the +5-year shift), and then read scripts/staging-plan.mjs as an executable object rather than as a document. Round 13 built that file specifically so an ordering defect would be caught mechanically. It caught N81. It could not catch what was inside it.

Battery: 474 falsifiers, 0 failing — at today's date and five years on. 39 new.

17.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N85BLOCKERthe queue gate and the vendor Worker form a bootstrap cycle — and the ordering proof could not see it, because its state tokens were coarser than the state they modelled
N86BLOCKERthe "MUST BE GREEN" gate exits 0 when it did not run, so the checkpoint was satisfiable by an unset variable
N87BLOCKERthe plan jumps to a CLICKHOUSE_URL nobody created — and ddl.sql creates a ROLE where CLICKHOUSE_USER needs a USER
N88HIGHthe gate certifies a vendor queue's DLQ and says nothing about who consumes it, or on what terms
N89MEDassertWrangler() was named in a comment and never written
GUARDMEDa manual plan step certified itself

Two more were found while implementing these, and both are recorded below because neither came from review: the "healthy account" fixture three rounds had been proving the green path with (§17.7), and a user name the plan and its generator spelled differently (§17.8).

The through-line is round 13's, one level up: the code has matured faster than the infrastructure bootstrap. Every finding this round is in resource creation, ordering, credentials or verification. None is in E's event semantics. Fourteen rounds and 474 falsifiers have still not produced a reason to replace Workers, Queues, Durable Objects or ClickHouse.

17.2 N85 — a proof over a vocabulary is only a proof about the world when the vocabulary distinguishes the states the world distinguishes

Round 13's order was:

create vendor queues + DLQs -> ... -> FULL queue gate MUST BE GREEN -> deploy cd-e-vendors

A vendor queue's dead letter queue, batch size and retry budget are properties of its worker consumer configuration, and that configuration comes into existence when the consumer Worker is deployed — not when the Queue and DLQ resources are created. So the gate required what only the step after it could provide. Reproduced against the shipped round-13 checker, in exactly the pre-deploy state round 13's own plan creates:

FAIL  e-events-amplitude-staging has exactly one dead letter queue (found NONE)
FAIL  e-events-amplitude-staging uses ITS OWN ... (found NONE)
FAIL  e-events-posthog-staging   has exactly one dead letter queue (found NONE)
FAIL  e-events-posthog-staging   uses ITS OWN ... (found NONE)

Four failures on an account with nothing wrong with it. This is N81's shape, inside the file built to make N81 impossible.

validatePlan() missed it because queues.vendors claimed to provide queue:vendor-dlqs, and that token means the DLQ resources exist, not the consumers pointing at them are configured. The model could prove an ordering about its own vocabulary and nothing more. The tokens are per-consumer now: the vendor deploy declares consumer:vendor-posthog and consumer:vendor-amplitude, and the full gate requires them.

The gate has a scope. predeploy certifies everything true before any Worker exists; full adds the vendor consumer topology. cd-e-vendors deploys first, between them — safe for a reason worth stating rather than assuming: nothing is producing messages yet. cd-e-ingest is the only producer and it is deployed two steps later, so a vendor consumer that is live and idle is exactly what is wanted. It exists so the gate can certify it.

And a scoped gate must name the subset it did not cover. predeploy returns a populated deferred list and prints it under a heading that says these are unchecked. Without that, a green pre-deploy run reads exactly like a green full one — which is N86's defect rebuilt inside the gate N86 is about.

17.3 N86 — absence of evidence had been encoded as successful evidence

$ unset CF_ACCOUNT_ID CF_QUEUE_TOKEN
$ npm run check:queues:staging
E queue configuration check — NOT RUN.
$ echo $?
0

So the plan's MUST BE GREEN could not distinguish every invariant holds from I checked nothing. It was especially reachable because round 13's plan had no step that created or exported `CF_QUEUE_TOKEN` at all — Cloudflare requires Queues Read and Write for an HTTP pull consumer, because ACK mutates queue state, so the credential the gate needs was one the plan never provisioned. cloudflare.auth is now step 1 and both gates require it.

A command named check may never return success for "not checked". The informational output was genuinely useful, so it kept its text and lost its verb: --describe prints it and exits 0, check without credentials exits 2. Two questions, two commands, two exit codes — and 2 rather than 1 because a caller must be able to tell the queues are wrong from I could not look.

The first run of the fixed gate exited 1. EXIT_NOT_RUN was declared beside its finding, two hundred lines below the await main() call, so the command whose entire finding is "this must not exit 0 when it did not run" died on

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'EXIT_NOT_RUN' before initialization

and exited 1 — still not 0, still wrong, and wrong in the way that reads as the queues are broken. It was caught because the round-14 falsifier spawns the script and reads the real exit code. A falsifier asserting EXIT_NOT_RUN === 2 would have passed against a script that crashed before reaching it. That is N67 once more: the gate's own execution is the thing to test.

17.4 N87 — a role is not a user, and the plan created neither

Round 13 claimed the plan ran from zero resources. Its config.ids step said to fill CLICKHOUSE_URL with "the ids the previous steps returned", and there was no previous ClickHouse step. The whole plan was queues, DLQs, a pull consumer, a gate, KV, config, secrets, Workers, traffic.

Underneath that, a second one. ddl.sql ends with CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS e_ingest and creates no database user. cd-e-flush authenticates over HTTP Basic as CLICKHOUSE_USER, and a ClickHouse role is not an authenticating principal — it is a bundle of grants that must be granted to a user. cd-e-flush/wrangler.toml made the conflation explicit:

CLICKHOUSE_USER      the `e_ingest` role — INSERT only (brief §11)

which names a role in the slot that holds a user. So CLICKHOUSE_USER had no value it could be filled with — not a wrong value, no value: the object it named was never created by anything here, and the DDL that should have created it carefully created something adjacent.

Four steps now: clickhouse.service → clickhouse.schema → clickhouse.ingest-user → clickhouse.verified. The user is not created in ddl.sql, deliberately: that file is committed and applied by hand, and a CREATE USER ... IDENTIFIED BY '...' line in it is either a placeholder somebody deploys verbatim or a secret in git. npm run clickhouse:principal:staging generates CREATE USER / GRANT role TO user / ALTER USER ... DEFAULT ROLE with a fresh password, prints it once, and stores nothing. The DEFAULT ROLE line is the easiest to omit and the hardest to diagnose: without it the login succeeds and every insert fails on a privilege the user demonstrably holds.

clickhouse.verified runs the flush's own preflight queries as the real principal, not a list invented for the step — N34 is the finding that a capability verified with a query the flush does not issue is a capability nobody checked. Two of the six read system.*, and whether a non-default ClickHouse Cloud user may do that is not settled here: ClickHouse's grant behaviour on system tables is inconsistent by engine (ClickHouse/ClickHouse#35239) and there is no instance to settle it against. Which is exactly why they are run rather than asserted. Both are marked DEGRADES rather than BLOCKS, because readVersion() and readDedupConfig() catch their errors and return null — a missing capability there does not fail loudly, it removes a check, and an operator who is not told will read silence as success.

17.5 N88 — "has a consumer" is weaker than "has the right consumer with the right failure semantics"

N83 taught this gate that has a DLQ < has the right DLQ. The next line was never written. A DLQ says where a failure lands and nothing about who failed. Reproduced against the shipped round-13 checker, with both vendor queues consumed by a Worker that is not ours, on settings that are not ours, with the correct DLQs:

ok: true   problems: []

A green gate over a topology in which nothing E wrote is running. The settings are not tidiness: max_retries is the vendor leg's entire durability budget and batch_size is what makes a fanout batch legal against the vendor's own limits — N37's lesson, on the vendor leg instead of on retention.

Two spelling traps came with it, and both are N82's shape:

wrangler.tomlCloudflare API
max_batch_size = 25settings.batch_size = 25
max_batch_timeout = 10settings.max_wait_time_ms = 10000 — seconds → milliseconds
max_retries = 5settings.max_retries = 5

A checker comparing the TOML number to the API number directly reads a correct queue as wrong by a factor of a thousand, and the natural fix for that — loosening the comparison — is how a gate stops being one. The map is written down and a falsifier drives the real TOML through it.

And the consumer's Worker name is itself ambiguous, so it is read as a set. Cloudflare's List Queues consumer object carries script; the Consumers subresource documents script_name; some SDK surfaces nest it under settings. Checked against the API reference 2026-08-24 and not resolved — the documentation genuinely shows more than one and there is no account to settle it against. Every spelling is read, and a consumer from which none resolves is a FAILURE: I could not determine who consumes this queue is not evidence that the right Worker consumes it. When a real account settles the spelling, narrow the list and record the date; do not leave it wide because it works.

17.6 N89 and the config guard — a claim nothing executed, and a step that certified itself

Round 13's comment listed the middle path as four things and shipped three. There was no assertWrangler() anywhere in the bundle; the only runtime use of a version was wranglerVersionNote(process.env.WRANGLER_VERSION) — a variable wrangler does not set — inside the no-credentials branch N86 has since established should not have been claiming anything. A function named in a doc comment is prose, exactly as a printed command is. It exists now, with an injected runner so the battery never spawns a process, and it stays a note rather than a refusal: a gate that refused to run on a version bump would be turned off, and a gate that is off catches nothing.

config.ids had no command and provides: ['config:ids'], and validatePlan() treated that as a fact. It is an intention. Some placeholders fail loudly — a bad KV id makes wrangler deploy refuse because the binding cannot resolve — but [vars] are plain strings Wrangler does not validate:

CF_ACCOUNT_ID  = "PLACEHOLDER-NOT-A-REAL-ACCOUNT-ID"
E_QUEUE_ID     = "PLACEHOLDER-NOT-A-REAL-STAGING-QUEUE-ID"
CLICKHOUSE_URL = "PLACEHOLDER-NOT-A-REAL-STAGING-CLICKHOUSE-HOST"

Those three deploy successfully and fail two hours later inside a cron trigger — the worst place for it, because a cron failure is observed by whoever is reading logs rather than by whoever ran the deploy. npm run check:config:staging refuses while any survives, and validatePlan() now rejects any manual step whose output a later step depends on unless a later check verifies it.

The placeholder sweep is scoped to the environment being deployed, and that is a decision rather than an oversight: wrangler deploy --env staging reads [env.staging.*], and production's [vars] are not read by it (N78). A sweep failing on those would make the first staging deployment impossible until production was also filled in — and a gate nobody can pass is a gate that gets removed. They are reported as notes instead.

17.7 The "healthy account" fixture was not a healthy account

Not from the review. Found while implementing N85 and N88, and the more uncomfortable of the two self-inflicted findings.

Rounds 9, 12 and 13 each built their own healthyAccount() and used it to assert the green path — assert.deepEqual(r.problems, []), "the correctly wired account is still green". None of the three contained a single dead letter queue as a resource, and none named the Worker consuming a vendor queue. Every DLQ assertion in the gate read a dead_letter_queue string off a consumer, and Cloudflare creates a queue with that name if one is absent — so the evidence was self-fulfilling, and the fixture agreed with the gate about what an account consists of while being the thing used to test the gate.

A fixture that models only what the code already checks cannot falsify the code's coverage — only its logic. That is N74 (a fake that cannot represent the mechanism reports the claim as proven anyway) pointed at the deployment gate's fixture rather than at the flush's fakes. It is also why N88 was reachable by a reviewer and not by the battery: the battery had no way to express the account N88 describes. One builder now, in test/queue-accounts.mjs, with preDeployAccount() alongside it — the state N85 is about, which nothing could previously express either.

17.8 A name stated twice is a name that can disagree

Also not from the review — found by reading the first printed plan. The plan titled its step create the e_ingest_worker USER from the bare constant while the generator emitted e_ingest_worker_staging. An operator following the plan would have created a user, been told a different name, and put whichever they trusted into CLICKHOUSE_USER. Derived from one function now. N73's rule about counts, applied to an identifier.

17.9 Still open — unchanged from §13.6

Round 14 adds nothing and removes nothing. Cross-batch event_id reuse, rate limiting, vendor_repair_v1's missing reader, the N31/N36 demotion, FNV-1a's collision resistance, manual site-key issuance, and N63's refusal cost all stand exactly as §14.7 left them.

The events_v1 25-month TTL is still unruled and must be confirmed before the first production event and before any privacy page quotes a figure (§DDL, round 2 N5).

17.10 The sequence, and the measurements that are still all question marks

npm run plan:staging prints it, order-checked, from zero resources:

Cloudflare auth (account + Queues READ/WRITE token)
  -> queues + DLQs -> canonical HTTP pull consumer (--message-retries 100)
  -> CHECKPOINT 1: check:queues --scope predeploy   MUST HAVE RUN AND BE GREEN
  -> ClickHouse Basic -> ddl.sql -> the ingest USER -> prove the USER can do the flush's work
  -> staging KV -> real config values
  -> CHECKPOINT: check:config   no placeholder survives
  -> secret files -> FIRST deploy cd-e-vendors WITH --secrets-file
  -> vendor consumers now exist
  -> CHECKPOINT 2: check:queues --scope full   MUST HAVE RUN AND BE GREEN
  -> deploy cd-e-ingest -> deploy cd-e-flush
  -> controlled synthetic traffic -> force duplicate / outage / lease cases
  -> measure ClickHouse

The table round 13 asked for is unchanged, and the local battery still cannot manufacture a single row of it:

MeasurementReal result
