The reviewer's judgement stands and this round agrees with it: stop reviewing the imaginary staging environment and make it real. What round 14 changes is that the sequence which does that is now one an operator can execute from zero without hitting a cycle, a missing component, or a gate that reports success for having done nothing.

18. Round 15 — bootstrap evidence closure

The round-14 reviewer accepted the architecture for the fifteenth time, reran both batteries (474/474, and 474/474 at +5y), and then asked a question round 14 had not: does the evidence each gate produces actually join to the thing it is evidence about?

Battery: 500 falsifiers, 0 failing — at today's date and five years on. 26 new.

18.1 The findings

#SeverityWhat it is
N90BLOCKERthe ClickHouse principal verifier printed queries that are not the ones the flush runs — and labelled the two most important ones the opposite of what the flush does with them
N91HIGHthe config gate proves an id's shape; the queue gate holds that id's true value; nothing joined them
N92BLOCKERthe plan's one "Cloudflare credential" is two different authorities, and the names it exports do not authenticate wrangler at all
N93HIGHthe gate never proved the runtime token can pull — only that it can list
N94MEDplan:staging reports success when wrangler cannot run

Every one of these is the same shape, and it is a different shape from round 14's:

verified query       <-/->  actual runtime query      (N90)
verified queue       <-/->  configured queue id       (N91)
operator credential  <-/->  operator operation        (N92)
runtime token        <-/->  runtime capability        (N93)
plan success         <-/->  executable toolchain      (N94)

Two true facts, no join between them. Round 14's findings were about what a gate checks; round 15's are about whether the thing checked is the thing used.

18.2 N90 — round 14 built this while fixing N87

N87 was "the plan verifies a component it never created". The fix added a ClickHouse principal verifier and hand-transcribed the flush's queries into it. The hand got it wrong twice.

the flush reads (ASYNC family — ASYNC_INSERT_SETTINGS is in force):
    replicated_deduplication_window_for_async_inserts
    replicated_deduplication_window_seconds_for_async_inserts

the verifier told the operator to run:
    non_replicated_deduplication_window        <- INVENTED. In no family at all.
    replicated_deduplication_window_seconds    <- the SYNC family's

So an operator could run every printed query, watch them all succeed, deploy, and have the flush refuse every drain. A verifier claiming to exercise the production query was exercising a different query — which is N34's finding exactly, rebuilt by the fix for a different one.

And the classification was backwards on the two that matter. Both were marked DEGRADES, and the generated instructions told the operator in so many words that "nothing downstream will ever complain". proveDedupPrerequisites() refuses the drain on either — supportsAsyncInsertDedup(null) !== true is refusal (a), dedup.blocks === null is refusal (b). The verifier stated the opposite of the truth about the one thing it exists to check. The reviewer is right about why the round-14 falsifier missed it: it checked that each entry named a source and regex-checked that the two readers contained catch. It never compared the SQL, and it never followed those caught nulls into the refusal branch.

The repair is not two corrected strings. dedupConfigSql(), versionSql() and probeCapabilitySql() live in insert.mjs; the runtime readers call them and so does the provisioning printer. A falsifier asserts the strings are identical — not equivalent, since equivalence is what a transcription claims — and captures what the readers actually issue.

The classification is no longer a label anyone types. test/round15.test.mjs drives the real flush with each capability denied and reads stopped_because. All three stop the drain. FakeClickHouse gained deniedQueries to make that expressible: it could model a column-scoped grant on events_v1 and could not model "this user may not read system.merge_tree_settings" — so no test could ask what the flush does in the state N90 is about.

Round 14's own falsifier had pinned the wrong answer and was green, because the code and the test agreed with each other and neither had derived the classification from behaviour. That assertion is replaced, with what it used to say recorded beside it.

The two zero-row INSERT canaries are typed expressions now (SELECT toUUID(...) WHERE 0) rather than SELECT * FROM system.numbers LIMIT 0 — the old form also tested access to system.numbers and a UInt64→UUID coercion, so a failure would not have meant what the operation is named for.

18.3 N91 — shape is not identity, and the evidence was already in the building

Round 14 was candid in the source: it checks shape and "does NOT prove any id is the right id". That became load-bearing the moment the queue gate started fetching the account. Filled with syntactically valid nonsense, the gate returned {ok: true, problems: []}.

This is worse than a typo. cd-e-flush builds its pull and ACK URLs straight from CF_ACCOUNT_ID and E_QUEUE_ID. A valid id belonging to a different queue in the same account does not fail to start — it makes the flush drain someone else's queue and ack someone else's messages. List Queues returns queue_name and queue_id in the same object, so the join is free.

check:config --bind performs it: account id, canonical queue name → queue id, KV namespace id, and the ClickHouse URL the principal was actually verified against (E_VERIFIED_CLICKHOUSE_URL) — because otherwise an operator can verify service A, configure service B, and every other gate stays green.

18.4 N92 — one name, two authorities

Round 14's step 1 said to export CF_ACCOUNT_ID and CF_QUEUE_TOKEN, then run wrangler queues create. Those do not authenticate wrangler. They are E's own variables. Wrangler reads CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN / CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID or the wrangler login OAuth credential; the CF_-prefixed names are on Cloudflare's deprecated list. On a clean machine the plan stops at step 2, and the name collision makes it read as a permissions problem rather than an authentication one.

The two authorities are also not the same size and must not become so:

  • OPERATOR — creates queues and KV namespaces, deploys Workers. Stays on the operator's machine. Never a Worker secret.

  • RUNTIME — Queues Read + Write on the canonical queue. Becomes cd-e-flush's CF_QUEUE_TOKEN and lives at the edge.

The tempting shortcut is widening the runtime token until it can also provision. That puts an estate-deploying credential at the edge — the opposite of what ddl.sql spends forty lines establishing for ClickHouse. Step 1 is now wrangler auth token, verified against the wrangler on this machine rather than against documentation.

Round 15's own falsifier caught two steps I had missed: consumer.pull and all three deploys run wrangler commands and were still requiring no operator authority.

18.5 N93 — listing is not pulling

This file already carried the admission, in N86's refusal text: "a read-only token passes this check and then cannot run the pull consumer it just certified." And that is what it did — the gate's entire provider interaction was a GET.

Checkpoint 1 is an unusually safe place to prove otherwise, and the reviewer is right that it is the only safe place: it runs before cd-e-ingest exists, so the canonical queue has no producer. A pull with batch_size: 1 exercises the write-side authorization and consumes nothing. It also proves the queue id, which is N91's join from the other direction.

A message returned at that point is a finding, not a pass — nothing should be producing yet.

18.6 N94 — could-not-determine-readiness is not success

N89 ruled that a version mismatch is a note, not a refusal, and that ruling was right: a gate that refuses on a version bump gets turned off. Round 14 then treated a missing executable the same way, printing "nothing below can run until it is installed" and exiting 0. A human reads the warning; an automation reads the number. plan:staging exits 2 now, and --describe prints the sequence anyway — the same split N86 made between check and describe.

18.7 Still open — unchanged from §13.6

Cross-batch event_id reuse, rate limiting, vendor_repair_v1's missing reader, the N31/N36 demotion, FNV-1a's collision resistance, manual site-key issuance, and N63's refusal cost all stand. The events_v1 25-month TTL is still unruled and must be confirmed before the first production event and before any privacy page quotes a figure.

One new open question, and it is a staging question rather than a local one. ClickHouse 26.2 began migrating toward a unified insert-deduplication hash (insert_deduplication_version), while current documentation still describes replicated retry dedup in terms of the main replicated windows. The local model now agrees with itself — the runtime and the verifier read the same settings — but which dedup regime actually governs the ClickHouse Cloud version we are given is not decidable from here. The right move is the one this round's lesson implies:

share the verifier with the runtime locally; discover the provider regime empirically.

Staging should report the exact service version and settings and exercise retry behaviour against them, rather than growing a more elaborate local model of what ought to govern.

18.8 The sequence

wrangler OPERATOR authentication  (wrangler auth token)
  -> create the RUNTIME Queues token — Read AND Write, and nothing else
  -> queues + DLQs -> canonical HTTP pull consumer
  -> CHECKPOINT 1: topology + THE TOKEN REALLY PULLS  (safe: no producer exists)
  -> ClickHouse Basic -> ddl.sql -> the ingest USER
  -> prove the USER can run THE FLUSH'S OWN prerequisite queries
  -> staging KV -> real config values
  -> CHECKPOINT: check:config --bind   every id joined to the account
  -> secret files -> FIRST deploy cd-e-vendors
  -> CHECKPOINT 2: the FULL queue topology, now that the consumers exist
  -> deploy cd-e-ingest -> deploy cd-e-flush
  -> controlled synthetic traffic -> measure reality

The measurement table is unchanged and still entirely question marks. The first number wanted back is the one the reviewer keeps naming: actual ClickHouse active minutes/day across the twelve two-hour flush windows, including cold resume and post-insert merge activity. That is what tells us whether the sleep/buffer cost thesis works at all.

Fifteen rounds and 500 falsifiers have still not produced a reason to replace Workers, Queues, Durable Objects or ClickHouse. The failure profile has changed completely: nothing this round was about event semantics, and nothing was about what a gate checks. It was all about whether two things that are both true are about the same object.
